OBJECTIVE
This article describes standard guidelines for use by all I&FS District Offices to customize their
own Pre-Installation Meeting Guides.
INTRODUCTION
Pre-Installation Meetings are held to bring together those people responsible for the successful
installation of a General Electric Gas/Steam Turbine unit.
The meeting objectives are as follows.
1. To discuss the information described in this installation plan.
2. To establish a mutual understanding of commitments.
3. To describe General Electric's installation support activities.
4. To establish a channel of communication during the installation period.
To accomplish these objectives, topics ranging from a point in time prior to shipment through
start-up will be covered.
Active participation and free exchange of ideas are encouraged at these meetings. GE
representatives from both Power Systems and Energy Services will be present and qualified to
answer questions and discuss matters of importance.
To maintain a common source of information available for future reference on the subjects
discussed during this meeting, it is suggested that the minutes of this meeting be recorded and
inserted at the end of this manual. Comments are welcome at any time.

TO THE CUSTOMERS OF GENERAL ELECTRIC
This Pre-Installation Planning document is furnished by General Electric as a guide for
installation and start-up of a Gas or Steam Turbine unit. It is not a complete instruction, but a
compilation of the major factors to be considered by Purchasers and their agents in planning for
an installation.
Installation and start-up of this type equipment is complex and involves numerous variables
related to the interface of the gas or steam turbine with the Balance of Plant (BOP) installation.
It is the responsibility of each Purchaser to develop a specific installation and start-up plan for
their unit. General Electric Field Engineers will be available to assist in this planning.
The information presented herein is furnished without charge as an aid for installation planning.
In no case should it be considered contractually binding or a complete list of all considerations.
The ultimate responsibility for installation and start-up of the turbine rests with the Purchaser.
General Electric's responsibility is limited to providing technical direction as defined under the
terms of the Equipment Contract.
I. INSTALLATION SUPPORT
An efficient, high quality installation requires Management, Labor, Supervision, and Technical
Direction to supplement the materials purchased. Installation management, labor and
supervision are the Purchaser's responsibility. Technical direction is provided by GE under the
terms of the equipment sales contract. All labor, supervision, tools and equipment that are
supplied under a separate installation contract should be coordinated with the technical data
and guidance provided by GE under technical direction.
The following description of Technical Direction of Installation (TDI) is an interpretation of the
equipment sales contract definition. It is General Electric's intention to provide Technical
Direction of Installation using this interpretation as a guideline.
A. Technical Direction of Installation (TDI) – Definitions
Technical Direction of Installation for Gas and Steam Turbine equipment is an active, on-
site service by General Electric providing engineering and technical guidance, advice, and
counsel to the Purchaser and agents, with the objectives of providing a technically correct,
high quality, safe installation. Work that is supervised, managed and performed by others
is audited, observed, evaluated, and reported, with comparisons being made to applicable
specifications, instructions, drawings, recommendations, current practices, procedures
and techniques of GE.
GE Energy Services

It is the Purchaser's responsibility to provide direct supervision, management, regulations,
arbitration and measurement of the Purchaser's personnel and agents regarding the
related work. The Purchaser is also responsible for planning and scheduling the work.
Guidance, advice and counsel provided to the Purchaser's personnel and agents in these
areas are considered to be aspects of technical direction regarding the proper and timely
installation and start-up of the gas or steam turbine equipment.
The GE representative providing TDI will be the primary contact for questions, problems,
etc., regarding installation. When technical direction has been suspended, the I&FS
District Office in __________ will act as the primary contact.
1. Technical direction provides full straight time service for a total period of up to ___
manweeks for the gas turbine and ___ mandays for the steam turbine. Straight-time
service is the first 8 hours of each shift, 5 days per week, Monday through Friday,
excluding recognized holidays. During those periods when no productive
installation work is being accomplished on the involved equipment, technical
direction may be suspended. One or more field representatives, as deemed
necessary by GE, will be assigned to provide the TDI function.
It is GE's intent to provide sufficient technical direction to cover the installation and
start-up activities, beginning with the setting of sole plates or other equipment
shipped in advance of the turbine, and ending with the completion of the installation
work and start-up activities.
2. If the installation schedule is delayed or extended, and the duration of up to ___
manweeks for the gas turbine or ___ mandays for the steam turbine is exceeded,
GE will render additional billing at GE's then-current Published Rates. When there
is no appreciable activity for periods in excess of 40 work hours, the field
representative(s) will be assigned to other jobs. In general, delays of this type most
likely occur:
a. Between arrival of equipment shipped early and preparation for setting of the
sole plates.
b. Between completion of the gas/steam turbine assembly work and plant start-
up.
Field service consultation will be made upon the Purchaser's request, and a field
representative(s) will be returned to the jobsite upon reasonable notice.
3. Travel and living expenses, brought about by reason of work extension and/or
suspension, will be billed at a published per diem rate.
GE Energy Services

4. If the installation schedule is accelerated and the overall job duration is shortened
by multiple shift operations, there will be no additional cost to the Purchaser for the
first 8 hours of each shift, 5 days per week, Monday through Friday. It is expected
that the Purchaser will provide sufficient labor force on each shift to obtain optimum
productivity within the above framework. GE will provide representatives to cover
each shift.
If the installation schedule is accelerated and the overall job duration is shortened
by overtime operations, the Purchaser will be billed in accordance with the
equipment sales contract, i.e., normally the premium portion of GE's then-current
Published Rates.
It is Turbine Contracts responsibility, in conjunction with Product Service Installation,
to decide what action should be taken on behalf of I&FS in all matters relating to
TDI. Contracts personnel will approach the customer as necessary and make all
contractual adjustments to the original equipment order. I&FS field representatives
will support contracts as requested, though recognizing that the TDI contract is
between the customer and the Turbine Department.
B. Technical Direction of Installation (TDI) – Responsibilities
GE considers its TDI responsibilities to be those associated with making the gas or steam
turbine unit ready for start-up and bringing the machine to full load. TDI participation in
the installation and start-up activities varies by installation as required to meet the stated
objectives of the project. The scope of this variation is largely determined by the requests,
capabilities, and constraints of the Purchaser and agents.
The installation and start-up of a gas or steam turbine encompasses a network of related
activities. Comments on consolidated groups of these activities are used here to further
define GE's and the Purchaser's obligations for TDI, and to clarify its scope.
5. Pre-Installation Meeting – A pre-installation meeting is normally held before
shipment of the major alignment components. The objective of this meeting is to
ensure that the Purchaser and the Installation Contractor fully understand their
responsibilities versus those of the Technical Director. Important items to review in
detail at this meeting are the agreed upon mutual commitments, the Purchaser's
installation schedule, the establishment of jobsite communication channels, the
Technical Direction Staff, etc.
6. Unloading Material – TDI includes providing technical information and counsel for
the unloading of all gas/steam turbine components at the location specified in the
equipment sales contract, plus observation and auditing of critical phases of these

activities. Technical information includes dimensions, weights, lifting locations,
special equipment, and GE recommendations.
7. Material Movement (i.e., skidding and cribbing of heavy components) – TDI includes
providing technical information and counsel for material movements, plus
observation and auditing of critical phases of the movements at the jobsite.
8. Examination of Material for Loss or Damage – The Purchaser or agent is
responsible for examining all incoming material for loss or damage. TDI includes
audit, verification, advice and counsel in all situations involving shortage, damage or
loss, and assistance in filing claims with the carrier. Observation and audit of the
unloading of major components includes attention to the condition of the material.
9. Inspection of Purchaser's Storage and Warehousing Facilities – The objective is to
ensure an adequate receiving, storage and dispensing system to avoid damage to
the stored material and compromising the installation plan due to losses or difficult
retrieval. Off-site or long term storage entails special circumstances and is not
normally included as part of TDI responsibilities.
10. Assistance in Maintaining Adequate Storage Records – TDI includes
recommendations on record keeping, explanations of GE documentation and
number systems, and assistance in identifying material.
11. Coordination and Administration of the Procurement of Tools and Equipment –
Guidance in this area is provided to avoid compromising the installation plan
because of items being unavailable at the proper time.
12. Checking of Foundation and Setting of Foundation Plates – TDI covers auditing of
elevations, foundation dimensions, bolt locations, provisions for piping and wiring,
potential interferences, and other similar details, plus technical guidance for and
observation of grouting of foundation plates.
13. Installation, Inspection and Assembly of the Gas/Steam Turbine and Associated
Equipment – This activity, consisting of several hundred actions, comprises the bulk
of the installation process. Timely auditing and observation are required in order to
provide TDI guidance, advice and counsel. Availability and utilization of technical
recommendations, instructions and specifications are confirmed. Deficiencies are
noted and corrections recommended. Engineering checks and data specified by GE
are obtained and evaluated. Procedures are observed and audited, and
modifications negotiated when necessary.

When alternate solutions are not acceptable, the Technical Director will advise the

proceed contrary to GE's recommendation.
14. Reviewing and Reporting of Schedules and Sequence of Installation – The
responsibility for preparation, review, and updating of the installation schedule lies
with the Purchaser or agents. The Technical Director will make recommendations
based on available information, and periodically report on the progress of the
gas/steam turbine installation as compared to the original mutually agreed upon
installation schedule. Acceptance of this advisory service varies by installation.
Therefore, GE will prepare a report to ensure that the Purchaser is continuously
aware of GE's evaluation of installation progress.
15. Inspection of Assembly, Clearances, Alignment and Cleanliness to the Extent
Possible without Dismantling – The Technical Director will observe and audit
activities which are the responsibility of the installation contractor whenever
necessary to ensure that results meet GE's specifications and recommendations.
Exceptions will be noted (in writing if necessary) and reported to the Purchaser for
resolution.
16. Installation and Placement into Service of All Supplier Equipment – Guidance,
advice, and counsel is provided to a supplier when considered desirable by the
Technical Director to resolve a problem.
17. Advice, Counsel, and Auditing of Fluid and Auxiliary Systems Flushing and Cleaning
Operations – The Purchaser or agent is responsible for installing and maintaining
clean fluid and gas/steam systems, and giving final approval of cleanliness. The
Technical Director will make recommendations based on procedures and flushing
equipment employed and the condition of filters, screens, and samples as observed.
18. Specialized Technical Direction Services – As part of TDI, GE will provide Start-up
Engineers to check and adjust control systems as required.
19. Completion of All Required Equipment Modifications – Technical Direction includes
keeping records of and advising the need for completion of all equipment
modifications recommended by GE after shipment. The Purchaser will be

It is important to set up proper facilities and procedures for receiving, inventorying, and storing

Installation efficiency is maximized when material is readily available at the required time. While

A. Arrival and Inspection
The Purchaser or agent is to inspect all material and equipment upon arrival at the
carrier's final delivery point. The inspection is to include but not be limited to the following.
1. Inspect the protective covering and packing for obvious damage during transit.
2. Inspect the "Hump Meters" and blocking of components on the transport vehicle for
indications of movement during shipment.

where special orientation had been requested.

delivery.
• Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) for HAZARDOUS material, and a packing list
for the equipment being delivered.

arranged in an accessible and convenient manner for further inspection and handling.

effective and efficient installation.

B. Material Inventory and Control
Following is the process for receiving MSD equipment and materials.
1. When notice is received from the supplier that equipment and materials are ready to
ship, GE will issue to the supplier a Notification of Shipping Release (NSR)
authorizing shipment to the job site. A copy of the NSR containing the information
listed below will be faxed to the Customer's Material Representative.
• Case Number
• Package Type (Case, Crate, Skid, Box)
• Weights and Dimensions
• Vendor Name
The most significant piece of information contained on the NSR is the list of Case
Numbers included in the shipment. Each case is assigned a number using a
systematic labeling method which specifically identifies the equipment and material
being shipped.
The first digit in the Case Number identifies the Unit with which the material is to be
used. The next four alpha-numeric characters identify the Model List Item (MLI)
number of the equipment. The last two digits are sequentially numbered (beginning
with 01) to identify the particular case. For example, the first shipping case for the
Inlet Duct Arrangement (MLI A041) for Unit No. 1 would be assigned the Case
Number 1A04101. If 16 cases were needed to ship the entire arrangement, the
remaining cases would be numbered 1A04102, 1A04103, etc. up to 1A04116.
Using this detailed, systematic labeling method helps facilitate receiving and
inventory processes, and can aid in planning site laydown areas.
2. The Bill of Lading (BOL) for each shipment received should list all the Case
Numbers included in that shipment. Each case in the shipment should have a
packing list on the outside and inside of the box. Upon receipt, the BOL should be
checked against the cases received to ensure that all equipment and material
intended for the shipment was actually delivered. Copies of the BOL and packing
lists should be provided to the GE TA Staff.

logic network when properly programmed allows all of the above, plus critical path
planning, periodic job tracking with compensation for manpower and material deficiencies,
job cost tracking, etc. The installation schedule used should be designed to meet the
needs of the specific installation and to provide optimum installation performance.

This document provides information concerning Gas Turbine reference materials and hyperlinks to tools
that should be used to assist the Gas Turbine Field Engineer in performing his or her duties.

Field Engineers. Unit-specific details are not provided in this document. All sketches and descriptions are
to be considered “Typical” within this document unless otherwise specified. This document is property of
General Electric and is considered Company Proprietary Information.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
The GI&FS Environmental Health & Safety Manual (EHSM) outlines the requirements that must be
followed on the job site during an installation or maintenance outage.
Safety, health, and protection of the environment must be an integral part of all business operations,
design, construction and start-up, and includes EHS planning prior to and during work to anticipate and
minimize hazards and incidents. Every reasonable effort must be made to create and maintain a safe and
healthy work environment at each customer site.
Where working conditions are not covered by these safety requirements and procedures, or when a
requirement or a procedure is not completely understood, obtain specific instructions or clarification from
manager, supervisor or EHS before proceeding with the work.
INTRODUCTION
This article provides information regarding historical Gas Turbine information, useful Web sites and various
information that may assist a TA to perform an installation or maintenance based job efficiently.

SECTION 4. UNIT RECORD SHEET
The Unit Record Sheet (URS) is an invaluable source of information which identifies all original drawings,
modifications and uprates for any Gas Turbine. The URS can be found on the Services Portal within the
Energy Services Applications hyperlink area. The link is identified as "COPICS – Unit Record Sheet".

SECTION 7. GAS TURBINE GLOSSARY
–A–
Abrasive Cleaning This is a turbine cleaning method where an abrasive cleaner such as nutshells are
injected into the turbine during operation under load. The nutshells remove harmful
deposits and restore 10 to 50% of a turbine's performance losses.
Absolute Separators Fuel cleaning devices that are configured in a vertical arrangement where the gas fuel
first enters vane sections to separate the larger droplets, then passes on to the
coalescing filters where the smaller liquid particles are removed. The coalesced
droplets form on the outside of the filter and are drained by gravity to a collection tank.
It is the similar to the Combination Separator except that the method of separation is
reversed. (See also Combination Separators.)
Accessory Package Where the generator and accessories are all in-line resulting in lower installation costs
and faster commissioning. Usually consists of the lube oil system and reservoir,
hydraulic oil system, fuel oil system, atomizing air system, gage cabinet, torque
converter and rotor turning device.
Accessory Compartment A sheet metal house with access doors. The Accessory Compartment may be on the
same base as the turbine or located on a separate base. It contains mechanical
elements necessary to support prime-mover operation.
Accessory Coupling Consists of several gears which drive most gas turbine accessories at proper speeds,
which connect the turbine to the starting device. The gear is driven first by the starting
device, then by the turbine when the unit reaches self-sufficient speed. This gear
drives the liquid fuel pump, water pump, main lube pump, main hydraulic pump and
main atomizing air compressor.
Accessory Gear Box This term refers to the casing for the turbine-driven accessory gear or to the actual
gear assembly.
Accumulator A hydro-pneumatic device designed to absorb a hydraulic shock and to deliver a
regulated force (in the form of pressure and fluid) during transient demands on a
system.
Actuator A self-contained device designed to deliver a controlled or regulated force in order to
put some other device in action, or to place another device at a required position.
Advanced Seals Found on the new H model gas turbine units, these seals have built-in brushes to
reduce leakage of air between the stationary and rotating sections of the turbine. Also
know as brush seals. (See Brush Seals.)
Alloy 706 This alloy is used to manufacture modern turbine wheels. It is extremely strong and
allows tighter tip clearances.
Ambient Temperature This is the temperature of the environment surrounding the turbine. It can be used to
calculate the turbine firing temperature.

Annular Combustor Shape and configuration-round and horizontal.
Annunciator The signaling apparatus of the protection system which annunciates (visually or
audibly) when a fault condition to the turbine and load device is sensed.
Air Extraction Process of taking air from the compressor discharge casing for other applications. This
results in a loss of power calculated to be 2 percent for every 1 percent of air
extraction. In general, up to 5% of the compressor airflow can be extracted from the
compressor discharge casing without modification to casings or on-base piping.
However, air extraction between 6 and 20% may be possible depending upon the type
of unit and the combustor configuration. In these cases, some modifications to casings,
piping and controls are in order. Any air extraction above 20% will require extensive
modification to the turbine casing and unit configuration.
Aircraft Derivative Gas Turbines that have their base design derived from the aircraft engines designed
and built in conjunction with GE Aircraft Engines, with headquarters in Cincinnati, Ohio.
Airfoil Shape Bucket shape designed to facilitate the most efficient use of energized air to spin the
turbine and create power.
Air Temperature One of the primary factors affecting gas turbine performance, ambient air temperature
affects the output, heat rate, heat consumption and exhaust flow. Each turbine model
has its own temperature effect curve which depends on the cycle parameters and
component efficiencies as well as air mass flow.
Annular Space The ring-like space between the combustion liner and the flow shield.
Atomizing Air Atomizing air is air separated into tiny fragments by high pressure and then delivered
to each fuel nozzle to finely atomize the fuel for complete, smoke-free combustion. The
system supplies air at a pressure higher than that in the combustor. The pressure drop
across the fuel nozzle sweeps the fuel into the air stream in a finely atomized spray
pattern. The major equipment in an atomizing air system are a compressor and pre-
cooler. In general, this system provides improved inlet temperature distribution, which
reduces maintenance of hot-gas path components.
Autoignition Temperatures The temperatures required for spontaneous combustion of gas fuels when there is no
(AIT) ignition source. Autoignition is an instantaneous ignition of liquid droplets in fuel
causing, in many cases, premature ignition of the pre-mixed gases in the turbine,
which is called "flashback." Due to this serious problem, GE specifies that no liquids be
in the gas fuel.
–B–
Base Load Defined as operation at 8,000 hours per year with 800 hours per start; or the maximum
temperature control set point above which the turbine cannot be operated with out
sacrificing turbine life expectancy.
Bellmouth A flared, bell-shaped inlet which provides an even air-flow distribution through the inlet
compressor through the inlet guide vanes.
GE Energy Services

Bearing Seal The general term used to identify the means of preventing oil leakage from a bearing
area. There are several types of seals; close tolerance and mechanical seals, plus a
pressure source to contain the oil after it is used to lubricate and prevent it from
leaking.
Bearings Bearings are machine parts in which another part (journal or pin) turns or slides.
Several types of bearings are used to support gas turbine rotors. These include journal
elliptical, journal tilting pad, thrust tapered land, journal cylindrical, ball bearings and
roller bearings. Bearings are pressure-lubricated by oil supplied by the main lubricating
oil system.
Black Start The capability to bring a "cold iron" machine on-line when a source of outside electrical
power is unavailable. The unit must be equipped with a diesel engine starting device. A
dc battery-powered turning device is used for rotor cool down to ensure integrity of the
black start capability.
Blade The rotating or stationery airfoils of an axial compressor. (See also Buckets.)
Borescope Inspection An optical borescope is used to visually inspect sections of the turbine flow path area
and compressor for gas-path damage. An effective borescope inspection program,
conducted at recommended intervals, can result in the removal of casings and shells
from a turbine unit only when necessary to repair or replace parts.
Brayton Cycle This is the thermodynamic cycle, named after George Brayton who discovered it, upon
which all gas turbines operate, characterized by two significant parameters: pressure
ratio and firing temperature. The pressure ratio is the compressor discharge pressure
divided by the pressure at the inlet. The firing temperature is thought to be the highest
temperature reached in the cycle. It is defined by GE as the mass-flow mean total
temperature at the first-stage nozzle trailing edge.
Brittle Term describing loss of resiliency in parent metal due to aging, extreme cold or
chemical exposure.
Broad-Frequency Banded-N Acoustical characteristics of the combustor volume.
Brush Seals These are advanced seals now available in industrial gas turbines to provide a tight,
rub-tolerant seal which experiences minimal degradation over time. The brush seal is a
bristle-like bundle of metal that bounces back to its original configuration after a rub.
They are attached to the inner barrel. These are used in the compressor discharge (or
high pressure packing) and the outer air seal on the number 2 bearing of certain gas
turbine models.
Buckets Also known as blades, these are curved vane elements mounted on the rotor and
encased in a shell or shroud. They are the interface with the hot gas path that transfers
the energy to the generator.

Bucket Coatings Coatings protect the bucket from corrosion, oxidation and mechanical property
degradation. They provide a surface reservoir of elements that form protective and
adherent oxide layers to protect the underlying base material from oxidation and
corrosion attack, and general degradation. There are several kinds of coatings used by
GE that have been divided into two basic types: diffusion-style called Platinum
Aluminide (PtAl) and an over-lay style such as PLASAMGUARD™ GT-29 IN-PLUS.
Bucket Cooling This cooling is achieved by air cooling holes drilled or cast into the buckets.
By Pass Valve The mechanical device that regulates the flow of fuel or air in either one of 2
processes: 1) as a fuel by pass on a liquid fuel system using a positive displacement
pump; or 2) as an air control valve used in pulsation protection systems.
–C–
<C> Designation for the Common Data Processor module, which is the communicator
between the operator interface and the turbine control processors (<R> <S> <T>) in
the SPEEDTRONIC™ Control System.
Can Assembly There are 3 main components in the can assembly: 1) combustion can cover; 2) flow
sleeve; 3) transition piece.
Cap and Centerbody The liner cap and centerbody contain the cups that accept the primary fuel nozzles
which are mounted on the can cover. The centerbody portion accepts the secondary
fuel nozzle. The area inside the centerbody is where the secondary fuel is pre-mixed
with combustion air.
Casing This is the protective tube surrounding the gas turbine rotor and is composed of a
series of cast-iron castings bolted together end-to-end. The two castings at the
forward-end are the inlet and compressor castings and are made of gray iron, while the
two at the aft-end are the discharge and turbine shell castings. These latter are
generally made of ductile iron, or steel castings, or fabrications.
Changeover Under Load The automatic changeover from one fuel to another while the unit is in operation.
Check Valve A valve that allows fluid to flow in one direction, but restricts or completely cuts off flow
in the opposite direction.
Centrifugal Pump This is a pump designed to use a rotating impeller in an enclosure to move liquid from
place to place.
CO2 Carbon Dioxide; used as a fire-extinguishing medium in a gas turbine.
Coalescing Filter These filters are used in conjunction with dry scrubbers when removal of practically all
liquid fuel droplets is required. The filter unit is comprised of a vertical pressure vessel
that contains a number of parallel tubular filter cartridges. The wet gas containing small
droplets flows through the filter where the droplets are collected and removed from the
filter by gravity, and flow into the sump.

Cogeneration Defined as the sequential production of necessary heat and power (electrical or
mechanical) or the recovery of low-level energy for power production, cogeneration is
an economical means of providing plant energy. Sequential energy production yields
fuel savings relative to separate production facilities. Cogeneration power is frequently
generated prior to the delivery of the thermal energy to the process, when, for
example, gas turbine exhaust energy is ultimately used for process requirements.
Combination Separators Fuel cleaning units that combine changeable filter elements with vane mist eliminators
in a single vessel. The gas passes through the filter elements where liquid particles are
coalesced and solids removed. Due to the coalescing effect, the vane is able to
efficiently remove more free liquid particles than either the dry scrubber of the vertical
gas separator alone. Often used instead of coalescing filters when high liquid rates are
anticipated. They are configured horizontally. (See also Absolute Separators.)
Combined Cycle One or more gas turbines with heat-recovery steam generators in the exhaust
sequence that produce steam for a steam turbine generator, heat-to-process, or a
combination thereof.
Combustion Liner The chamber in which chemical energy is released and added to the gas flow. (Modern
combustion liners are slot-cooled rather than cooled through use of the older louver
system.)
Combustion System In the gas turbine, this system consists of a multiple-chamber assembly composed of
three basic parts: the fuel injection system, the cylindrical combustion liner and the
transition piece.
Combustor The gas turbine section where large quantities of fuel and air are mixed and burned. It
is comprised of a fuel injector(s) and walls to contain the flame.
Compressor Gas Turbine section where air is compressed to appropriate pressure before entering
the combustor where it is mixed with fuel and ignited.
Compressor Blades These are the individual air foils on the compressor wheels and casings, attached to
the rotor or casings by dovetails. There are two kinds of compressor blades, inlet guide
vanes and variable guide vanes.
Compressor Discharge The keystone of the gas turbine, the casing contains the last stages of the compressor
Casing stator blades. The discharge casing supports a bearing, joins the compressor and
turbine stator; supports the forward-end of the combustion wrapper and provides inner
support for the first-stage turbine nozzles.
Compressor Rotor This is the rotating section of the compressor which consists of blades and disks.
Compressor Stator The section of the compressor that is comprised of a casing and stationary blading.
Control System The mechanical and electrical equipment designed to provide safe start-up and shut-
down of the gas turbine and load.
GE Energy Services

Cool Down Period This is the period of time that the turbine rotor needs to slow or stop after shutdown.
Normal cool-down periods vary from five hours on the smaller units to up to 48 hours
on the largest ones. The cool-down can be interrupted at any point to restart the
turbine.
Cranking of Turbine Term used to describe the slow turning of the turbine rotor at start-up or cool-down
period, generally at a maximum of 20% speed.
Crossfire Tubes The pipes that connect combustion chambers on multiple combustion turbines. The
tubes allow flame propagation from the two spark-plug ignited combustors to the other
chambers.
Cooling & Sealing Air A system which provides air pressure necessary for cooling and sealing various turbine
components.
Cooling Water System A system that provides a supply of water necessary to cool certain gas turbine
components.
Crude Fuels Unrefined fuels such as petroleum.
–D–
Dedendum The distance of a gear tooth from the pitch line to the bottom of the tooth.
Diaphragm Located between the turbine wheels and attached to the inner diameter of the nozzle
assemblies, these barrel-like structures prevent the working medium from escaping
past the inner side walls of the nozzles and rotor. They are used in all stages except
Stage #1.
Dilutent Injection Water or steam injected into the combustion liner to assure the desired level of NOx.
Dovetail Bottom part of the bucket or blade that attaches it to the compressor or turbine wheel;
of various shapes designed to hold through tremendous centrifugal forces.
Dry Acid Deposits Deposits of sulfates and nitrates that travel, often hundreds of miles, before landing on
the ground.
Dry Low NOx (DLN) A system of nitrogen oxide emission control that utilizes combustion techniques based
upon multiple combustion staging to optimize fuel/air ratios. The combustor design
allows fuel and air to be "lean-premixed" in various combinations to achieve the
desired operating temperature to meet needed emission levels. Two additional ways to
control nitrogen oxide emissions are through catalytic clean-up of NOx and CO from
the gas turbine exhaust, and steam or water injection. (Also see NOx, steam injection,
and water injection.)
Dry Scrubbers See Scrubbers, Dry

–E–
Electrostatic Precipitation This process uses charged particles to remove oil particles from an air and oil mixture.
Emergency Lube Oil Pump This is a back-up pump to be used if the main lube oil pump fails or ac power is
unavailable for startup or shutdown. It uses a dc battery motor.
Emissions Control There are three primary methods for controlling gas turbine emissions: 1) injection of
water or steam into the burning zone of a conventional combustor; 2) Catalytic clean
up of NOx and CO from the gas turbine exhaust; 3) design of the combustor to limit the
formation of pollutants in the burning zone utilizing by utilizing "lean-premixed"
technology.
Evaporative Cooler Best used in hot, low humidity climates, evaporative cooling decreases the compressor
inlet temperature to improve output and heat rate in a gas turbine. Effectiveness is a
measure of how close the cooler exit temperature comes to approaching the ambient
wet bulb temperature.
Exhaust Air System The network that directs the used air aft of the last stage to the atmosphere. This
system also incorporates a silencing module to reduce the sound level of the released
gas. The two air systems most commonly used are the straight-up and the switch-back
types.
Exhaust Frame The component that usually supports the aft-most journal bearing. Its shape slows
down air discharged from the last range of buckets, recovers some of the pressure and
directs the air to the turning vanes. The exhaust frame has internal struts that are air-
cooled to maintain the bearing cavity position.
Exhaust Stack The exhaust assembly which can include silencing sections.
–F–
Fire Protection System The system designed to detect and extinguish a fire if one occurs in an external turbine
compartment area.
Fired Hours The number of hours a particular gas turbine has been in operation.
Firing Temperature Thought to be the highest temperature reached in the firing cycle, or the mass flow
mean firing temperature at the stage 1 nozzle trailing-edge plane. (Brayton Cycle)
Each increase in firing temperature yields dual benefits: increased efficiency, i.e., lower
fuel costs; and increased specific work, i.e., higher output per unit of air flow, which
reduces capital cost. Gas turbine power generation systems, with continually updated
design engineering, have demonstrated the ability to evolve to even higher firing
temperatures.
First Stage Also known as the "Primary Zone" the first stage is where fuel from the primary nozzles
in either burned or mixed with combustion air depending on the operational mode of
the unit. It is this stage where the mixing of fuel and air helps produce a cooler flame
hence lower NOx.

Flame Detectors The machine parts that sense the presence of flame during startup by utilizing the ultra
violet rays generated by the flame. Four types of detectors can be used: an ultraviolet
sensor, an infrared sensor, a thermocouple, or a thermopile.
Flash Point This is the lowest temperature at which the vapor above a given fuel will ignite when
flame is applied. The flash point indicates the degree of fire hazard associated with
handling the fuel.
Flexible Couplings Type of couplings used with an Accessory Package that simplify field installation and
allow the assembly to be more tolerant of variations in alignment.
Flow Divider (liquid fuel) Fluid motor device comprised of a series of positive displacement gear elements that
equally divide the flow of fuel to the fuel nozzles. Sometimes started by an electric or
hydraulic motor, it then becomes self-sustaining. It sometimes contains a magnetic
pick-up to aid the control system in measuring liquid fuel flow.
Flow Sleeve Helps direct the desired quantity of compressor discharge air for combustion or cooling
within the combustion can.
Flue Gas Scrubber These are used to reduce sulfur oxide emissions by contacting the flue gas with a
sorbate composed of metal (usually sodium, magnesium, or calcium) hydroxides in
solution which acts as a base to produce sulfate and sulfite precipitates.
Forward Compressor Case The housing that contains the early stages of the stator vanes. It provides a flow path
for the air and assists in the formation of an air extraction manifold.
Fretting Wearing away of metal as it rubs against another metal, generally associated with
press fit or close fitting parts.
Fuel Injection System The fuel injection system delivers fuel to the combustion zones. The Dry Low NOx 1
combustor has two types of fuel nozzles: primary and secondary.
Fuel Nozzle This is the device that supplies fuel to the combustion chamber. Various types of
nozzles are used; there are single-fuel nozzles for either liquid or gas, and there are
dual fuel nozzles. On gas fuel systems, orifices in the fuel nozzle meter the gas to the
combustion chamber. Most modern turbines utilizing liquid fuel have a high-pressure
air source called atomizing air, that is piped into the nozzle to help control smoke
problems associated with liquid fuel.
Fuels The two most frequently used fuels in gas turbines are natural gas and distillate oil.
Natural gas produces approximately 2 percent more output than distillate oil, although
there are many variables that can increase oil's output and efficiency. Other fuels that
can be used are non-distillate liquid fuels such as crude and residual oils, or lighter
liquids such as naphtha, kerosene and methanol. GE gas turbines are also capable of
burning low-heating value gases such as syngas and steel mill gas, as well as land fill
gases. Each unit must be approached individually and fuel systems adjusted
appropriately to achieve maximum performance.
Full Load The designated (rated) output at ISO conditions (base-load at ISO condition).

–G–
Galling A defect caused by the movement of two surfaces in contact with each other.
Gas Path Normal flow path of air through the gas turbine.
Gas Turbine Compartment The housing that contains the prime mover and, on some units, the accessory base as
well. It is usually a sheet metal structure with access doors mounted on an "I" beam
base.
Gasification The process of turning various types of coal into a gas fuel for use in the gas turbine.
Gas Separator A device used to remove liquid fuel droplets (slugs) from fuel before it enters the
turbine, which operates on an inertial separation principle. Wet gas passes through an
inlet baffle and then through a series of angled vanes that impart inertial forces on the
remaining liquid droplets, which are caught on the vanes and removed from the fuel
flow by the force of gravity. Gas separators are available in either vertical or horizontal
configurations.
Gear Pump This is a positive displacement pump that consists of a drive gear and driven gear
mounted in a suitable housing. The working medium travels from the intake port
around the outside of the gears to the outlet port.
Generator One of several load devices driven by a turbine. It is usually located at the aft-end of
the turbine on a separate base. It is air or hydrogen-cooled and usually has a terminal
voltage of 13.8kV. Available in various KVA ratings.
Generator Drive The term used to describe a gas turbine installation in which the driver load is a
generator providing electric power.
Gib Key One of the devices that prevents lateral or rotational movement of the turbine while
allowing axial and radial thermal expansion. The Gib Key is a machine part that is an
integral part of the lower half of the exhaust frame. Fits into the guide block. (See also
Guide Block.)
Guide Block One of the devices that prevents lateral or rotational movement of the turbine while
allowing axial and radial thermal expansion. The guide block is a steel block welded to
the turbine base, the gib key fits into the guide block, which also has adjusting bolts for
axial and transverse location of the turbine. . (See also Gib Key.)
Greenville, SC USA Current location of GE's Gas Turbine Manufacturing Facility.
–H–
H Gas Turbine The latest in GE's evolutionary family of heavy duty gas turbines, the advanced H
machine has broken the barrier to a 60% net efficiency power generation system with
this gas turbine-steam turbine combined-cycle system. The first H technology system
is expect to be tested in 1998, and be in commercial service before the end of the
decade.

Heat Exchanger/Cooler The heat transfer equipment used to extract excessive heat from one working fluid and
transmit it to another non-working fluid for eventual dissipation to atmosphere.
Heat Rate Measured Btu/kWh or Btu/hph or kJ/kWh (ck these caps)
Heating & Ventilating System A series of components, fans, heaters and thermostats used to control the
temperatures of various compartments.
Heating Value A fuel's heating value has a significant impact on performance. Factors influencing
heating values are fuels, pressure ratios, volume, water and air content, etc.
Heavy Duty Gas Turbine A GE heavy duty gas turbine is defined as a turbine (any frame size) built by the Gas
Turbine division of GE Power Systems. They are available in either 50 or 60 Hz
machines.
Hertz (Hz) International frequency equal to one cycle per second.
Honeycomb Shrouds These utilize a honeycomb material made of high temperature, oxidation resistant alloy
material with a 1/16th cell size and a foil thickness of 1 or 2 mils located on the
stationary shroud. The rotating bucket seal teeth with a cutting edge will cleanly cut
away the material when contact occurs. This design allows tight clearances to be
maintained during steady state operations.
Hot Corrosion Occurs on buckets as a result of alkali metal contaminants such as sodium and
potassium reacting with sulfur in the gas turbine fuel. There are two types of hot
corrosion: high- temperature (Type 1) and low-temperature (Type 2). Both are rapid
and often aggressive forms of corrosion. Lines of defense against hot corrosion are: 1)
reduce contaminants; 2) use corrosion resistant materials; 3) apply coatings that
improve the corrosion resistance of the bucket materials.
Hot Gas Path The gas turbine system that consists of the combustion chambers, transition pieces
turbine nozzles, buckets and exhaust section.
Humidity Effect The effect of humid air, which is less dense than dry air, on gas turbine output and heat
rate is especially evident on larger machines. Previously this effect was thought to be
too small to be of consequence, but in the larger turbines where humidity is used to
bias water and steam injection for NOx control, this effect has greater significance.
Hydraulic System The hydraulic system is designed to provide a clean, high-pressure source of hydraulic
pressure necessary to control various devices. In some unit designs, air entering the
gas turbine inlet is cooled to increase the density of the air mass. Air-cooled generators
can use a pre-cooler to lower the inlet air temperature. The atomizing air system uses
a pre-cooler to control the entrance air temperature to the main atomizing air
compressor.

Ignition Sequence This process consists of turning on ignition power to the spark plugs in the combustor
and setting the firing fuel flow. When flame is detected by the flame detectors, ignition
and cross-firing has occurred.
Inlet Air System The inlet air system is the means used to provide distortion free air in the correct
quantities to the gas turbine. Most turbines use some form of filtration to clean the air.
Some inlet systems cool the air mass by evaporative coolers, while other systems
protect the air mass from ice formation by treating the inlet air.
Inlet Chiller A device that uses coolant and coils to transfer heat in the compressor inlet areas.
Usually causes considerable condensate and is somewhat inefficient as most of the
cooling energy of the unit goes to condensation with little left to reduce temperature.
Inlet Cooling To improve output and heat rate, the compressor inlet temperature can be cooled
(lowered) by the installation of evaporative coolers, or an inlet chiller, in the ducting
downstream of the inlet filters.
Internal Voting Logic System of checks in the automated turbine control system whereby the computers use
a two-out-of-three voting redundancy system to monitor a gas turbine's performance.
Inlet and Exhaust Losses Air filtration, silencing, evaporative coolers, or chillers placed in the inlet or exhaust
heat recovery devices cause pressure losses in the system. The effects of these
losses are unique to each design and must be considered on each individual unit.
Inlet Guide Vanes (IGVs) Inlet Guide Vanes (IGVs) are devices used to control the inlet air flow through the
compressor. Their position therefore changes the air flow as a function of turbine
speed, ambient temperature and exhaust temperature. They are of variable geometry
and are designed to direct air at the optimum flow angle for the highest efficiency and
output. They are located at the aft-end of the inlet casing bellmouth in the compressor.
Inlet Filtration Used where required to filter air for sand, salt and other airborne contaminants before it
enters the gas turbine.
Inlet System The system that allows ambient air with low velocity to flow over interior surfaces. The
system is usually manufactured from low carbon steel.
Intersegment Seals The gaps between segments of shrouds and nozzles are a significant source of hot
gas leakage. Intersegment seals, or spline seals are comprised of strips of metal
placed in grooves on the segment faces. These have traditionally been used to form a
barrier to leakage between segments. Spline seals in gas turbines are rounded and
allowed to pivot in the groove. These are referred to as a "dog-bone" or "Q-Tip" seals
because of their appearance, and they provide the flexibility needed to adjust to the
thermal stresses in the gas turbine. There are other types of seals such as the
"pumpkin tooth" and "bus bar" seals which, when implemented, reduce leakage
significantly in some machines. Each unit must be evaluated and designed for the most
appropriate seals.
GE Energy Services

–J–
Journal The axis of bearing contact.
Journal Bearing The machine part that improves stability and absorbs the load of the rotating shafts
during normal operation. Various styles are used; see applicable unit instruction book.
–K–
–L–
Labyrinth Packing A seal designed with multiple rows of alloy teeth, located at the extreme end of the
bearing assemblies. Sealing air is circulated between the shaft and the seal to prevent
oil from passing the seal and spreading along the shaft.
Load Range A selected mode of operation within the designed load capability. For example, the
turbine may operate between spinning reserve and pre-selected load; the load range is
selectable.
Louvers Devices on the combustion liners which provide a film cooling on the inner surface of
the liner.
Lube Filter A device that filters the lube oil prior to its delivery to the bearings and gears.
Lube Oil Heat Exchanges Devices which allow the hot lube fluid to be cooled by heat transfer to the cooling
water.
Lube Oil Pumps Located on the accessory base/oil reservoir; includes an accessory gear-driven main
pump, an ac motor-driven auxiliary pump and a partial-flow dc motor-driven emergency
pump.
–M–
Master Control Switch The switch used by the operator to start and stop the machine. This switch can also be
used to select predetermined loads once the unit is running.
Magnetic Pickup The device that produces frequency (proportional to speed) output signals which are
converted into dc voltage signals. These signals are used for speed control or tripping
the turbine.
Main Hydraulic Supply Pump A very high-pressure pump that uses the common oil supply tank as its source. It is
usually a constant pressure, variable type, accessory gear driven, servo-supply pump.
Main Lube Pump The source of all lubricating oil pressure under normal operating conditions. It is a
positive displacement gear pump and accessory gear driver.
Maximum Load The absolute capability of the generator as listed in the design data. The unit maximum
load limit may be set by the load gear.
GE Energy Services

Field Engineer's Manual – Gas Turbine EM 5006
January 10, 2006
Subject Gas Turbine Reference Guide Page 41
Moisture Separator Removes moisture from the condenser.
Mist Eliminator A mechanical device that removes small oil droplets from the oil tank vent system prior
to the discharge of the vapor to atmosphere.
Monitoring & Diagnostics This is the process of accessing, transmitting, evaluating and reporting on the
(M&D) operating condition of power generation equipment. An effective M&D program
provides access to multiple users regardless of where they are located.
Multi-shaft One of two configurations available in the combined-cycle power generation equipment
line. (The other is the single-shaft.) A multi-shaft system is composed of one or more
gas turbines and heat recovery steam generators (HRSGs) that supplies steam
through a common header to a separate single steam turbine unit.
–N–
Natural Gas One of two preferred fuels for modern gas turbines; the second fuel is distillate oil.
Natural gas is the cleanest fuel used in gas turbines, it is composed mostly of
methane, with trace hydrocarbons such as ethane, propane, butane or hydrogen.
Nozzles Nozzles are GE's term for the stator vanes in a gas turbine. They direct the hot gases
towards the buckets.
Nozzle Segment An assembly of a small number of nozzle partitions. Several nozzle assemblies
comprise a complete nozzle assembly.
NOx Oxides of Nitrogen (NO and NO2, collectively called NOx) must be carefully controlled
to meet environmental requirements. This may be accomplished in three different
ways: 1) by the injection of water or steam into the combustion system; 2) by catalytic
clean-up of the gas turbine exhaust; 3) by designing the combustor to limit formation of
pollutants in the burning zone (Dry Low NOx combustion techniques). There are many
variables to successful control: for example, the amount of water or steam must be
adjusted for fuel flow, fuel type, ambient humidity, and the nitrogen oxide emission
levels required by the regulations in force at the site. (See also Water Injection, Steam
Injection and Dry Low NOx.)
–O–
Off Base A unit component not mounted on the accessory turbine or generator base is said to
be "off base."
Offset Ratio The amount of emissions must be offset in a new facility, as required by the Clean Air
Act of 1990.
On Base This term describes a unit component mounted on the accessory turbine or generator
base.
GE Energy Services

Subject Gas Turbine Reference Guide Page 42
Olefins These are troublesome unsaturated hydrocarbons such as ethene, propene, butene,
etc., that have a tendency to form deposits on fuel system surfaces. Owners should
identify the presence of olefins in potential fuel, take the necessary steps to reduce or
eliminate them, and get specific GE recommendations for reducing combustion
hardware fouling.
Overspeed Bolt The primary trip on a unit without an electronic trip system. This bolt senses an
overspeed condition and is mounted in the accessory gear box or on the turbine and/or
compressor stub shaft. It is also used as a back-up for an electronic overspeed trip.
Ozone Sunlight, summer temperatures, hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen produce ozone.
–P–
Parasitic Flows Defined as cooling and leakage air flows that bypass the combustion system; parasitic
flows can typically consume up to 20% of the total air flow through the gas turbine.
There are two categories: chargeable and non-chargeable. Chargeable is any air flow
which bypasses the combustion system and reenters the flow-path downstream of the
firing temperature calculation plane Tf, i.e., just downstream of the stage 1 nozzle
throat. Since output and efficiency are reduced, the losses are "charged" against the
thermodynamic cycle performance. Non-chargeable flows also bypass the combustion
system, but they reenter the flow path upstream of the firing temperature calculation
plane and are available to perform work. These non-chargeable flows do not impact
output, but do have a small impact on heat rate. Both types of parasitic flows impact
emissions as they reduce the amount of air available for combustion.
Particulates These are composed of smoke, ash, ambient non-combustibles, and erosion and
corrosion products.
Partition Airfoil-shaped stator section of the turbine nozzle assembly.
Peak Load Defined as operation at 1250 hours per year with five hours per start. Running at peak
load produces more power, but reduces life expectancy of turbine parts.
Peak Reserve Condition of severe operation that dramatically reduces the life of the hot section
turbine parts.
Performance Degradation There are two types: recoverable and non-recoverable. Recoverable performance
degradation is associated with compressor fouling and can be partially rectified by
water washing, or more thoroughly, by opening the unit and mechanically cleaning the
compressor blades and vanes. Non-recoverable performance degradation is due to
increased turbine and compressor clearances and changes in surface finish and airfoil
contour. Performance can only be recovered through replacement of affected parts.
Performance Verification Performance Testing is done as soon as possible after a machine goes on-line,
preferably while in "new and clean condition" which is considered to be less than 100
hours of operation. Power, fuel, heat consumption and sufficient supporting data are
recorded to enable as-tested performance to be corrected to the condition of the
guarantee. Instruments are inspected and calibrated, and tests are conducted as
described in the ASME Performance Test Code, PTC-22-1985.
GE Energy Services

January 10, 2006
Subject Gas Turbine Reference Guide Page 43
Plenum, Inlet or Exhaust An enclosure in which the volume of contained (inlet) air or exhaust gas (exhaust) is
under different pressure than that which surrounds the enclosure.
Pressure Ratio In the Brayton Cycle, the Pressure at the compressor discharge point divided by the
pressure at the compressor inlet point.
Pre-Mix Lean This is the term given to the process of mixing a large portion of the compressor
discharge air with the fuel just prior to combustion, creating a "lean mixture" that
produces low gaseous emissions when combusted in a fluid mechanics- stabilized gas
turbine combustion chamber.
Pre-Mixed Combustion This is part of the DLN process where the fuel and air are injected into the combustion
chamber and mixed together upstream from the flame zone, prior to ignition.
Pour Point The lowest temperature at which a given fuel oil will flow under standard test
conditions.
–Q–
–R–
<R> <S> <T> Designations for the three control processors in the GE SPEEDTRONIC™ suite of
control computers.
Rainbow Tests These are tests conducted on customer's unit components with new materials installed
side-by-side with the older or baseline materials to compare the results. Rainbow
materials are removed and evaluated periodically, then replaced with standard parts.
Rainbow tests can included bucket and nozzle coatings, combustion components and
bucket and nozzle materials.
Reaction Zone Area in the combustion liner where fuel is mixed with compressor discharge air and
then ignited.
Regenerator Heat Exchanger that transfers heat from the exhaust gas to the working fluid before the
gas enters the combustor.
Residence Time Amount of time hot gases are in the combustor.
Residual Fuels Low-grade by products of fuel refinement, these are fuels with low-hydrogen content
that create heavy smoke.
Ring Seal This seals the bearing area to prevent oil loss. Usually used in conjunction with an air
pressure source and labyrinth seal.
Rotating Seals These seals minimize leakage between stationary and rotation components in the gas
turbine. They must be tight, and yet allow for the probability of high speed contact
between the components. Two types of rotating seals are honeycomb and brush seals.
(See Brush Seals and Honeycomb Shrouds.)
Rotor This is the term applied to the compressor and/or turbine rotor assemblies in a gas
turbine.
GE Energy Services

–S–
Scaling, geometric In turbine design, geometric scaling is based on the principle that one can reduce or
increase the physical size of a machine while simultaneously increasing or decreasing
rotational speed to produce an aerodynamically and mechanically similar line of
compressors and turbines.
Secondary Fuel Nozzle Delivers fuel to the secondary combustion zone. The secondary nozzle is inserted into
the centerbody of the liner and may have a secondary flame detector mounted on it.
Selective Catalytic Reduction This is a system that converts NO and NO2 in the gas turbine exhaust stream to
(SCR) molecular nitrogen and oxygen by reacting the NOx with ammonia in the presence of a
catalyst. This system is restricted to units with a heat recovery boiler installed in the
exhaust, and it requires that temperatures remain within a narrow range. The SCR is
comprised of metal segments stacked in the exhaust duct that have a honeycomb
pattern with passages that are aligned in the direction of the exhaust gas flow.
Selector Valve This is a manual valve that allows pressure sampling on each fuel line going to a liquid
fuel nozzle. Incorporates an extra connection for specific customer selected pressures.
Servo Valve This is a flow-control valve designed to provide directional and proportional flow control
in response to the polarity and magnitude of a low-power, direction-current input signal.
The valve normally is used as a flow-control device in a closed-loop circuit to control
the direction and rate of movement of a piston actuator or other control device.
Scrubbers, Dry These are used to clean and condition gas before it enters the turbine combustor. Dry
scrubbers are multiple-cyclone (multi-clone) inertial separators that remove both liquids
and solid materials without using scrubbing oils or liquids. They come in vertical or
horizontal configurations, with the vertical ones typically used for the relatively small
flow volumes for a single gas turbine, and the horizontal units used to treat the gas in a
gas pipeline with high flow rates.
Shank The section of turbine bucket between the platform and the dovetail.
Shutdown Normal shutdown is initiated by the operator and is reversible until the breaker is
opened and the turbine operating speed falls below 95 percent.
Shrouds Shrouds are strips of metal opposite the bucket tips that limit air flow leakage. There
are stationary shrouds and rotating shrouds. The stationary shrouds are used on older
gas turbines and rotating, interlocking tip-shrouds are used on the newer turbines.
Simple-Cycle This is the process in which the working medium passes successively through the
compressor, combustor and turbine. Simple-Cycle units lack the heat recovery steam-
generator, and efficiencies are achieved with higher pressure ratios at given firing
temperatures. High-firing temperatures increase the power output at a given pressure
ratio, but at the sacrifice of efficiency.
GE Energy Services

COMPANY PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
Field Engineer's Manual – Gas Turbine EM 5006
January 10, 2006
Subject Gas Turbine Reference Guide Page 45
Single-Shaft This is a type of gas turbine where the rotating components, the compressor balding,
and the turbine blading are all on one shaft in an in-line arrangement. One of two basic
configurations available in the combined-cycle GE product line. (The second is the
Multi-shaft.) This machine is comprised of a single gas turbine, one heat recovery
steam generator (HRSG), one generator and one steam turbine.
Site Elevation Another factor that affects gas turbine performance is the elevation at the site.
Corrections are made for altitude and barometric pressure, as less dense air reduces
the airflow and output proportionately. Heat rate and other cycle parameters are not
affected by site elevation.
Slugging Heavier hydrocarbons in gas form liquid slugs that create problems with standard
combustor gas turbine units. These need to be removed by cleaning or treating the fuel
before the gas enters the turbine, otherwise they cause major hot gas path damage.
Soft Nozzle This type of primary nozzle uses an internal orifice to meter gas flow instead of
openings at the tip. This design helps reduce pressure oscillations.
Solenoid Valves Normally, two-position electrically actuated devices that will allow or prohibit fluid flow.
Spacers These are the spaces between the turbine wheels that provide access for the turbine
nozzles.
Specific Gravity (Fuel) This is the ratio of the weight of a given volume of fuel oil at 60° F (16° C) to the weight
of an equal volume of distilled water at the same temperature. (The closer the specific
gravity of the fuel is to that of water, the more difficult it is to treat it.)
Spinning Reserve The minimum load control point based on generator output.
SPEEDTRONIC™ Control There are several versions of this GE designed control system in current use on all
Systems types and sizes of steam and gas turbines. They are designated by the name Mark
and then a Roman numeral; e.g., Mark I through Mark V. SPEEDTRONIC Control
Systems are constantly being improved and are used to monitor, control and regulate
unit operation. On gas turbines, control systems perform many functions including fuel,
air and emissions control; sequencing of turbine fuel and auxiliaries for startup,
shutdown and cool down; synchronizing and voltage matching the generator and
system; monitoring all turbine, control and auxiliary functions; and protecting against
unsafe and adverse operating conditions.
Spline Seals See Intersegment Seals.
Staged Combustors Used to control emissions, staged combustors allow only a portion of the flame zone
air in the combustor to mix with the fuel at lower loads or during start-up. There are two
types of staged combustors: fuel-staged or air-staged.
Starting Device The machine component used to produce adequate torque to meet the requirements of
the starting system. Six types of starting Devices are used: diesel engine, electric
motor, steam turbine, natural gas expansion turbine, turbine impingement, and air
motor.
GE Energy Services

Subject Gas Turbine Reference Guide Page 46
Starts and Hours Criteria GE maintenance requirements are based upon independent counts of starts and hours
in a given turbine; whichever criteria limit is reached first determines the maintenance
interval.
Stationary Seals Leakage barriers around and between stationary components are called stationary
seals. They are typically metal-to-metal seals providing minimal clearance between
adjacent hardware parts. Areas where stationary seals are used include intersegment
gaps in shrouds and nozzles, the transition piece to the stage 1 nozzle interface, and
interfaces between shrouds and nozzles and support structures. (See also
Intersegment Seals.)
Stator A casing or group of casings surrounding a rotor assembly. Names that apply to the
various sections include: inlet casing, forward compressor casing, aft-compressor
casing, compressor discharge casing and exhaust frame.
Steady State Constant mode of operation.
Steam Injection Steam injection for power augmentation can be introduced into the compressor
discharge casing or the combustor. GE gas turbines are designed to allow up to 5% of
the compressor airflow for steam injection. The system is designed to allow only
enough steam to meet NOx abatement until the unit reaches base load.
Synchronization As a turbine approaches running speed, synchronization is initiated. This is a two or
three step process that consists of matching turbine generator speed, and sometimes
voltage, to the bus and then closing the breaker at the point where the two are in
phase within predetermined limits. When synchronization has been completed, the
turbine will be at a spinning reserve load.
–T–
Transition Piece The interface between the combustion system and the stage 1 nozzle; this is a major
source of non-chargeable leakage.
Thermocouples Thermocouples are temperature sensors that are invaluable to the safe and efficient
operation of a turbine. They can be placed in obscure places to measure temperatures
where it would be difficult or impossible to do so by other means. In the gas turbine
thermocouples are used to measure temperatures in wheel spaces, lube oil systems,
inlet, exhaust, and compressor discharge areas.
Tie-bolts Tie-Bolts are large bolts used to fabricate the compressor rotor.
Trips Turbine trips (shutdown of the turbine) occur when the protective functions of the
control system act as a result of detecting such events as overspeed, overtemperature,
high rotor vibration, fire, loss of flame, or loss of lube oil pressure. Additional features
on the more modern systems include monitoring combustion and thermocouple
operation, high lube-oil header temperature, low-hydraulic supply pressure, multiple
control computer faults, and compressor surge for the aircraft-derivative gas turbines.
GE Energy Services

Triple Redundant Controls State-of-the-art control system composed of three microprocessor-based computers
that share control of the gas turbine using triple redundant sensors. When one
computer or sensor fails, the triple-redundant system automatically switches turbine
operation, using internal voting logic, to the two remaining control computers and
associated sensors. Alarms alert the operator of a fault in the system. After the repair,
the two remaining computers interrogate the repaired system to ensure that it is
functioning properly.
Turbulators Drilled or cast swirl patterns in bucket cooling holes, giving more surface contact for
cooling air.
Turbine Wheels These are disks that are part of the gas turbine shaft. Buckets (or blades) are attached
to the wheels. They may be cast or slip-on type.
Turbine Rotor Flexibility The ability of the rotor to synchronize and respond appropriately to changes in
temperature and speed.
Turning Gear A cooling rotor or a rotor undergoing maintenance needs to be turned periodically to
prevent bowing, which will cause vibration upon subsequent startups. Turning of the
rotor for cool down or maintenance is done by a ratcheting mechanism on smaller
turbines and by a conventional turning gear on larger machines. The turning gear can
be operated manually or be attached to the accessory drive gear.
–U–
Ultra Violet Flame Detector These provide an indication of flame, or lack thereof, in the combustor. They utilize
ultra violet radiation. Usually two scanners are used.
Upgrade Refurbishing an older turbine with the most modern design parts and components, to
increase output.
Uprate Refurbishing a turbine to increase MWs.
–V–
Variable Inlet Guide Vanes See Inlet Guide Vanes.
Viscosity (Fuel) Viscosity of a fluid is a measure of its resistance to flow and is expressed in units such
as Saybolt Universal Seconds (SSU) or Saybolt Furol Seconds, or Kinematic Viscosity
Centistokes (cSt).
–W–
Water Injection Water is injected into the head of the combustor for NOx abatement. This increases
mass flow and therefore, output. However, the amount of water is limited to that
required to meet the NOx requirement, as water injection will also increase operating
costs and inspection intervals.
GE Energy Services

Water Washing Water washing is a turbine cleaning system that removes ash deposits from
combustors and turbines using a spray-soak-refire method. Water is sprayed into the
combustors and turbine through the atomizing air manifold and nozzles while the unit is
operated on the staring motor, and allowed to soak into the deposits. The unit is refired
and the water soaked deposits form steam with sufficient pressure to remove the
deposits.
Washing, Fuel Ash forming fuel oils are generally contaminated with water-soluble salts of sodium and
potassium which can be removed by mixing heated fuel with 5 to 10 percent potable
water and a small amount of emulsion-breaking fluid. The procedure consists of an
extraction process followed by the separation of salt-laden water from the fuel.
Wax Content (Fuel) Wax in fuels such as crude oil and heavy distillates will clog the fuel system unless it is
kept below its melting point. The percentage of wax and its melting point must be
determined and heating and heat tracing methods incorporated to ensure that the wax
is continuously dissolved.

directly to the installation site as MSD equipment. These are vendor drawings managed
through a system called VENDOC.

to the installation site as MSD equipment. These are also VENDOC drawings.

Subject Use of Gas Turbine-Generator "Customer Drawings" Page 1
GENERAL
Typically 6 to 12 weeks after receipt of a unit order, Gas Turbine Requisition Engineering will
issue a package of drawings and specifications commonly called "Customer Drawings,"
"Customer Design Documents," or "Customer Interface Drawings." These documents are listed
by Model List Item (MLI) number in two groups for typical MS6001B/MS7001EA gas turbine-
generator units. See Table 3 of EM 5016, Installation Documents for MS6001B Gas Turbines.
Standard documents are documents which are "always" supplied and are contractually
committed to be supplied.
Supplementary documents are drawings which are not optional, but are not part of the
contractually committed items. Depending upon the specific unit configuration, some or all of
these documents may be supplied.
STANDARD "CUSTOMER DRAWINGS" CONTENT SUMMARY
MLI 0301 – Outline, Gas Turbine Package Conn-Electrical
• Locates junction boxes, receptacles, and electrical devices requiring field
interconnection.
• Locates grounding studs.
• Suggests cable routing through embedded conduit (MLI 0323) and entry points.
• Used in conjunction with Foundation Interface Outline (MLI 0323) and Diagram,
Block, Cable (MLI 0463).
MLI 0306 – Outline, Mechanical – Gas Turbine and Load
• Provides overall Gas Turbine-Generator (GT-G) unit dimensions and arrangement.
• Provides reference dimensions for all centerline equipment packages.
• Provides dimensions of Gas Turbine-Generator supplied equipment which extends
from the centerline packages.
• Provides space removal requirements for maintenance purposes (e.g., generator
rotor, tube bundles, etc.).
Issued by: I&FS - Methods Scheduled Review: January 2005

Note: The terms "supplements" or "used in conjunction with" imply a primary
relationship, meaning that information contained in these documents needs to
be used and correlated.
NOTES AND CAUTIONS ON USE
Because of a number of factors including lack of familiarity of users, changing product
arrangements and packaging, special applications, etc., problems have occurred in using these
documents. A combination of experience and specific drawing study is needed to fully interpret
the engineering and construction implications.
The following are common areas of confusion.
• Most of the drawings include a mixture of information, and a specific drawing may need to
be referenced by mechanical, electrical and civil/structural engineering groups.
• Due to the present use of supplemental documents, many drawings may need to be
referenced in order to obtain complete information about a specific area.
• Differences exist in scope of supply. For example, Gas Turbine supplies pipe and
electrical cable for some of the off-base equipment (e.g., Exhaust Frame Blowers,
Demister and Gas Fuel Module), but supplies only the skid for most off-base systems.
• Foundation design, foundation embedments, and sub-sole plates are usually the
responsibility of others, with Gas Turbine supplying only interface requirements and
specific recommendations.
• Although Gas Turbine supplies shim packs for support of the various packages, the sizing
and procurement of sub-sole plates (as well as all foundation embedments) is usually the
responsibility of others. It should be noted that dimensions given in the details of the
Foundation Interface Outline (MLI 0323) are for the pads or sole plates of the equipment.
The sub-sole plates may need to be larger, or can be smaller, depending on the size of
shims, attachment of axial positioning block, etc.
• Although Gas Turbine recommends the size (diameter), height above sub-sole plate, and
material of the anchor bolts, the remainder of the bolt design and the procurement is
usually the responsibility of others.
GE Energy Services

COMPANY PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
Field Engineer's Manual – Gas Turbine EM 5017
February 11, 2003
Subject Use of Gas Turbine-Generator "Customer Drawings" Page 7
• Drawings listed under MLI 0323 sometimes carry the MLI 0323 identity in the title block,
which can mislead a user into thinking that all of MLI 0323 is represented in a single
drawing. The "A" size "top drawing" must be referenced to determine the full list of
required drawings.
• In some cases, Gas Turbine supplies the electrical cables but does not define skid
location or conduit runs. This requires feedback to Gas Turbine during the requisition
phase to allow required sizing of the length for these cables.
• Although Gas Turbine does not locate many of the off-base skids, there are design
constraints which must be considered in the final equipment arrangement (e.g., distance
of skid from unit pipe connections, distance from nearby obstructions, etc.).
• Drawings with "suggested" or "recommended" information should be regarded with extra
caution, as sometimes the "Max. Case" is represented which may be excessive and costly
for specific unit needs (e.g., conduit runs in the main foundation).
• Gas Turbine uses a more conservative fill rate on conduits (e.g., a 25% fill of a 4-inch
conduit as maximum vs. the industry standard of 40% fill).
• Although not noted on the drawings, additional "straight through" conduit runs should not
be above the recommended due to heat from the exhaust plenum.
• Drawings listed under MLI 0326 may have their own separate and different MLI Numbers.
• Although titled as foundation interface drawings, both MLI 0326 and MLI 0330 are lists of
skid and module drawings that contain more information than just foundation interface.
• Piping schematics contain more than just piping or fluid flow information (e.g., relative
location of instruments, etc.), and should be regarded as system schematics.
Note: The term "off-base" is used to mean support separate from the main centerline
foundation.

Subject MS 6001B Lube Oil System Field Assembled Piping Page 1
INTRODUCTION
This procedure is a guide to help Field Engineers when assembling the Lube Oil Piping on an
MS6001B gas turbine split base unit. This piping is Material Shipped Direct (MSD) from the
vendor to the site.
REFERENCE DOCUMENTS
No. Description
ML 0969 Piping Arrangement, Base Interconnect
ML 0969 Piping Arrangement, Interconnect – Lube Oil
ML 0969 Piping Arrangement, Interconnect – Fuel Gas
ML 0905 Piping Arrangement, Lube Oil Feed and Drain – Base
ML 0906 Piping Arrangement, Lube Oil Feed and Drain – Load
LUBE OIL PIPING ASSEMBLY PROCEDURE
The following procedure is a proven method of installing and assembling the 18 inches square
Lube Oil drain manifold located on the left side of the accessory and turbine bases.
1. Inventory MSD crates marked ML 0969 and ML 0906 when delivered to site. This is the
Customer's responsibility. Store parts in a clean, dry location.
2. Report shortages or damaged parts to appropriate product department
3. Rig and move the 4 segments of the 18 inch square drain pipe (Figure 1) and set down
along the left side of the turbine and accessory bases.
4. Set Segment #3 of the drain pipe in position next to the turbine base on wood blocking. It
must be set on the blocking because the two IGV tubing connections coming out of
Junction Box #2 must line up with the two IGV tubing connections coming out of the
turbine base side wall. See Figures 2 and 6.
Note: Assemble the 4 inch dresser coupling on the pipe coming out of the turbine base
before setting the square drain pipe in position. This must be done in order to
attach the coupling (see Figure 6).

Post-Installation meetings are held to help ensure that General Electric equipment is operating
properly, that the Punch List items are promptly acted upon, and that the Customer is satisfied.
