CONDUIT/DUCT BANK NOTES
1. Conduit which have been cut are to be reamed to remove rough edges and burrs.
Metallic conduit is normally threaded at both ends, unless otherwise noted.
2. Generally conduits are to project 3 inches above the finished floor or grade, and 3 inches
beyond the finished wall, except for conduits entering switchgear from below which should
not extend more than 1 inch above finished floor.
3. Buried, intermediate or rigid metallic conduit are to be at least 18 inches below grade,
unless protected all around with corrosion resistant material or encased in a 2 inches
concrete envelope.
4. Buried, non-metallic conduit are to be a minimum of 18 inches below grade, measured
from the top of the conduit or 12 inches below grade if a 2 inch concrete pad (or
equivalent physical protection) is placed in the trench over the underground installation or
just below grade if protected under a 4-inch thick concrete slab which extends at least 6
inches beyond the conduit in either direction.
5. Buried, non-metallic conduits, used for installation of 600V or higher voltage service in all
cases, are to be enclosed in a concrete envelope of at least 2 inches thick.
6. Under areas of heavy vehicular traffic, the depth for conduit should be 2 feet or greater
and are to be encased in reinforced concrete.
7. It is recommended that when concrete is used to encase conduit that it be identified by
red coloring, (e.g., red dye placed on or in the concrete).
8. Flexible conduit is normally limited to a length of 18 inches with a maximum length of 36
inches.
9. Intermediate or rigid metallic conduit 1 1/2 inch diameter and smaller can be bent in the
field. Use of factory fabricated elbows is recommended on all intermediate or rigid
metallic conduit greater than 1 1/2 inch diameter.
10. Should additional conduit be added to the main centerline foundation, reference should be
made to MLI 0323 for minimum depth required for conduit running under the exhaust
plenum. A minimum depth of 24 inches is typical to prevent overheating.
11. Before pouring foundation verify that embedment restraints are not touching conduit, (to
prevent direct conduction of heat to conduit) and that conduits are capped at both ends.

12. Installed conduit is never used as a ground conductor for welding.
BURIED POWER CABLE NOTES
1. A sand cushion of at least 6 inches thickness should be compacted in the bottom of the
trench before laying the first row of cable.
2. The cable should be laid with a slight snaking to prevent overstressing upon earth settling
and thermal movement during load cycling. Power cables of the same level may require
spacing to allow for needed heat dissipation, look for specific recommendation on
associated drawings.
3. The sand which is backfilled between the lower and upper rows of cable should be well
compacted before laying the upper rows in order to minimize its settling. Care must be
taken in order not to damage the lower cables.
4. After carefully compacting the 6 inches of sand covering the top row of cables,
creosotecoated planking, unglazed tile, or a 4-inch concrete slab should be placed above
the cable runs for mechanical protection as well as to warn workmen of its presence.
5. Suitable above ground markers are to be installed to indicate the cable run.
6. Refer to the applicable construction drawings for the specific cable routing as well as
depth and spacing dimensions.
7. The orientation and spacing of the cables shall strictly follow the arrangement shown on
the construction drawings.
GROUNDING NOTES
1. All non-current carrying metallic objects such as switchyard structures, fencing, building
steel, equipment enclosures, pullboxes, support structures and other frame work, shielded
cable sheaths, metal conduit, pipe, etc. are to be grounded to a common earth potential
whether or not specific details of such appear on the construction drawings. Typically two
#4/0 conductors are used.
2. Building steel and fencing are to be grounded at intervals not exceeding 70 feet - 0 inches
unless indicated otherwise. Normally small skids are grounded at two opposing corners.
Turbine-Generators generally provide 2 grounding lugs per compartment.
3. Metallic conduits are to be connected to the ground grid at one end only. The connection
to the ground grid must utilize a ground cable.
GE Energy Services

COMPANY PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
Field Engineer's Manual – Gas Turbine EM 5120
January 28, 1991
Subject Electrical Installation Practices Page 8
4. All equipment ground connections must be electrically continuous from the equipment to
the ground grid.
5. All equipment and structures are to be grounded utilizing a visible ground connection at
the equipment.
6. The equipment grounding conductor may be a metallic raceway such as steel conduit or
tray or a cable. Equipment ground cable may be bare or insulated. If it is insulated, it
must have a green colored insulation. If green cable is unavailable the cable used must
be colored green with tape or paint, or stripped bare over the entire portion that is visible.
7. All grounding grid cable must be bare and must be buried 18 inches below grade unless
indicated otherwise; it must be laid slack to prevent damage due to soil settlement.
8. All grounding grid cable riser "pigtails", for connection to a structure, should extend a
minimum of 1 foot - 0 inches above the base of the structure.
9. All buried ground grid connections are to be made utilizing an approved compression type
fitting or by an approved exothermic process, such as brazing or soldering.
10. No ground connections to be buried should be covered over prior to the consent of the
project engineer/manager of his appointed representative.
11. All above grade ground connections are to be made utilizing approved connectors with
non-corrosive bolts, nuts and washers unless indicated otherwise.
12. All ground cable connections are to be made after the connection contact surface is
thoroughly cleaned of dirt and oil to ensure a good low resistance connection.
13. Ground cables are not to be run through metal conduit or through metal barriers unless all
phases or polarities are included in the conduit or unless the ground cable is securely
bonded at both ends of the pipe, conduit or metal barrier.
14. Conduit sleeves for ground cable penetrations are to be of a non-metallic material.
15. Typically the grounding system should have a measured nominal resistance, with respect
to remote earth, of 2 Ohms or less. If this resistance is not attained by the system shown
on the construction drawings, advise the project engineer/manager for further direction.

Subject Gas Turbine Field Marked-Up ("As Installed") Drawings Page 1
INTRODUCTION
Many "As Manufactured" drawings supplied with Gas Turbine equipment require field changes
or revisions during the installation and start-up phases, or during Field Modification Instruction
(FMI) work completion. It is essential that these changes be documented in accordance with
this instruction (EM 5185) so that all necessary revisions can be accurately identified, approved
and incorporated into the revised drawings.
Until recently, the practice of modifying "As Manufactured" drawings involved marking prints
using only Black Ink. In an effort to improve the readability of marked up prints, all changes are
now required to be made using a Color Coding system. Color Coding Instructions are detailed
on page 3 of this instruction.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
In all cases, the Health, Safety and Environmental Manual (HSEM) will be the document
followed on the job site during installation, maintenance and repair of equipment.
Safety, health, and environmental protection must be an integral part of all department business
operations, including design, construction, start-up and maintenance. Every reasonable effort
will be made to create and maintain a safe and healthful work environment at each customer
site.
GENERAL INFORMATION
"As Installed" drawings are "As Manufactured" drawings that have been marked up in the field
to reflect the actual "As Installed" hardware configuration. Upon completion, they are to be
returned to Installation and Field Services (I&FS) for review and subsequent reissue and
distribution as revised "As Installed" drawings to correctly reflect the "As Installed" configuration.
These drawings normally fall into one of two general categories (defined as Category I and
Category II).
"AS INSTALLED" DRAWING CATEGORIES – DEFINITIONS
Category I
Drawings furnished as part of the Field Installation documentation package, which are
returned from the field as marked up "As Installed" drawings, and which reflect (via the
mark ups) the actual "As Installed" configuration of the unit or station. These drawings are
then returned to the I&FS Installation Engineer.

Subject MS 6001B Load Gear Contact Check And Field Inspection Page 1
INTRODUCTION
This instruction outlines the field engineering procedures to be followed when inspecting
MS6001B Gas Turbine Load Gear.
The inspection procedures provided in this article cover the general condition of the gear teeth,
gear tooth contact between the pinion and bull gear, cleanliness inside of the gear housing and
correct flow pattern of lube oil nozzles.
DESIGN INFORMATION
The Load Gear provided with the MS 6001 Gas Turbine is an up-over, double helical, high
speed design which places the high speed pinion gear shaft (that connects to the MS 6001B
Gas Turbine) above the lower speed bull gear (that connects to the generator). (See Fig. 1).
This procedure is based on the Philadelphia Gear S674-A gear assembly. (Philadelphia drawing
03031-2457). This procedure is also applicable to Westech load gear assemblies that have
been provided for some MS 6001 Gas Turbine units.
INSPECTION RECOMMENDATIONS
The load gear inspection should be performed during a gas turbine maintenance inspection.
Whenever possible, the generator coupling should remain bolted to the bull gear during the
inspection to add loading on the teeth, thereby improving the accuracy of the contact check.
When the contact inspection is found to be less than 75 percent (of the face area), a second
contact check is recommended to verify that the findings of the first check are accurate. If the
contact is still found to be less then 75 percent, the vendor should be contacted for their
evaluation and recommendations.
SPECIAL TOOLS, FIXTURES AND MATERIALS
The special tools and fixtures furnished by General Electric during the initial installation will be
required for load gear inspection. These include the field fabricated gear turning tool (or
coupling wrench), and the alignment centering ring provided by the manufacturer (when re-
alignment is necessary).
The special materials required to conduct a gear contact inspection include a tube of Prussian
Blue or Dykm Blue (not Layout Blue which dries), a tube of Permanent Artist Oil Yellow Paint –
Cadmium Yellow Medium, and a pint of parts cleaner such as alcohol or red dye check liquid
penetrant cleaner. Diesel oil, kerosene, and similar oily fluids do not produce satisfactory results
because the leave oily residue.

Method of Inspection
The following is the recommended method for inspecting the MS 61B load gear pinion and
bull gear shafts tooth contact–mesh alignment.
1. Insure that the turbine-generator and auxiliaries are properly tagged and locked-out.
2. Remove the inspection cover from the left upper side of the load gear case (some
newer gear cases may have the inspection cover on the right hand side.) (See Figs.
2 and 3).
NOTE: Prior to checking the contact, the direction of rotation and active (driving) tooth
faces of the driving gear (pinion) must be determined. (See Fig. 4)
3. Select five or six teeth on the active meshing faces of both the pinion and bull gears,
and thoroughly clean the teeth areas with a parts cleaner. (See Figs. 5, 6 and 7–
Detail “A”).
4. When all dirt, grease and oil are removed, apply a very thin coating of yellow paint
to four or five of the pinion gear shaft teeth on both helices. The coating must be
applied with a soft cloth, not a brush. (See Figs. 8 and 9–Detail “B”).
5. A very thin coating of Prussian Blue or Dykm Blue is then applied to four or five of
the bull gear shaft (driven rotor) teeth on both helices using a soft cloth, not a brush.
(See Figs. 8 and 9–Detail “B”).
NOTE: It is essential that the coatings be applied evenly along each helix and not
exceed 0.001 inches (approximate) in thickness. An excessive thickness of
coating will result in a contact pattern with little or no value.
6. Rotate the gear set through mesh, by jogging the starting means torque converter.
Do not roll the gears more then once through each application of colors.

7. Analyze the alignment according to the following criteria:
A. If the gear shaft internal alignment is correct, the transfer of yellow onto the
blue will be even and full across both helices. (See Fig. 10).
B. If the transfer of yellow onto the bull gear is not uniformly distributed, there are
three basic patterns which indicate gear misalignment that is near the limit of
normal operation. (See Fig. 11, Sketches A, B and C):
Sketch A Heavy yellow (or contact) at the base of the helix and at the apex
of the other, indicates internal misalignment. This is the most
common finding.
Sketch B Heavy yellow (or contact) at the base of both helices indicates
very slight difference in the helix angles between the pinion and
bull gears.
Sketch C Heavy yellow (or contact) at the apex of both helices indicates a
very slight difference in the helix angles between the pinion and
bull gears.
Sketch D Under full load, the yellow (contact) for each of the three
misalignment conditions (shown in sketches A, B and C) will be
more evenly distributed across the helices but the contact will not
be full or completely even as a normal transfer contact pattern.
(See Fig. 10).
NOTES: No correction of misalignment conditions are possible in the field.
The helix angle difference indicated in these examples is
extremely slight, and correction by re-cutting is not considered to
be necessary.
The distribution of paint contact indicated in these sketches does
not apply to high ratio gearing.
Record Contact Inspection
The contact check and inspection should be documented as follows:
1. Photograph the gear contact checks, to provide records for comparison with future
inspections.
2. Redraw the Gear inspection Report Form as required to accept the tape strip
records. (See Fig. 12).
3. Carefully place transparent tape strips (1 to 1-1/2 inches wide) over the contact
pattern left on each active tooth face, and gently press to transfer the pattern to the
tape strip. Slowly lift each tape and apply it the report form.
4. Complete the gear tooth condition reports. (See Figs. 12 and 13A and 13B).

REASSEMBLE INSPECTION COVER
1. Using a parts cleaner, thoroughly clean the colorings applied to the teeth of the active
meshing faces of the rotors.
2. Apply a bead of red RTV to the inspection cover (or install a new gasket where used), and
reassemble to the left (or right) upper side of the load gear.
3. Make up cover bolting. Refer to the vendor service manual for torque values.
Note: The gear case bolt holes should be filled with red RTV. The purpose is to fill the void
around the bolts and seal the bolt heads, preventing oil leagage from the casing flang
through the bolt holes, which may occure after load gear inspection.

INTRODUCTION
This article outlines the field engineering procedures to be followed when inspecting the MS
6001B gas turbine load gear.
This article covers load gear casing rigging and disassembly, pinion and bull gear shaft
inspection, journal bearing inspection, alignment fixturing, and re-assembly of the load gear.
DESIGN INFORMATION
Load Gears provided with MS 6001B Turbine Generator Sets are an up-over, double helical,
high speed design which places the high speed pinion gear shaft (that connects to the MS
6001B Gas Turbine) above the lower speed bull gear that connects to the generator.
This gear type is known as a S674-A Load Gear (Philadelphia Drawing 03031-2457.) They are
currently supplied by Philadelphia Gear, however this procedure also applies to Westech Load
Gears that have been provided for some MS 6001 Gas Turbine units. (See Figs. 1 and 2).
INSPECTION RECOMMENDATIONS
The load gear inspection should be performed during a gas turbine maintenance inspection. A
gear tooth contact check should be conducted prior to disassembly of the load gear/generator
coupling. Refer to EM 5210 for the GE approved procedure.
The load gear vendor must be requested to be at site during the bearing inspection if the gear is
still in warranty. The load gear vendor should be consulted if any abnormal conditions are
encountered during an out-of-warranty bearing inspection.

SPECIAL TOOLS AND FIXTURES
The special tools and fixtures furnished by General Electric during the initial installation will be
required for load gear inspection. These include the field fabricated gear turning tool (or
coupling wrench), the alignment centering ring provided by the manufacturer (when re-
alignment is necessary), and the field fabricated load gear clamp fixtures. Other tools necessary
for the inspection include the alignment fixture (provided in ML A033), and a Master Level
(Model 98).
STANDARD TOOLING REQUIREMENTS
Standard tooling will be required to remove bolting on the gear box flanges. The rigging
equipment required to disassemble and remove upper cover, pinion gear shaft and upper gear
box housing include; cables, nylon straps, shackles, 10 ton chain fall, two 1-1/2 ton
come-a-longs, torque wrench (with a range 0–900 ft. lb.), and a 1-1/2 ton port-a-power.
METHOD OF INSPECTION
The following is the recommended method for inspection of the MS 61B Load Gear main
bearings and journals at both ends of the pinion and bull gear shafts.
1. Before disassembly of the couplings start, insure that the turbine-generator and auxiliaries
are properly locked out and tagged.
2. Remove the inspection cover from the left side of the gear box and perform a gear tooth
contact check inspection. (Refer to EM 5210 for recommended procedures.) Some newer
gear cases may have the inspection cover on the right hand side. (See Fig. 3).
Gear Enclosure Disassembly
The gear enclosure roof must be removed in order to disassemble and inspect the load
gear shaft journals and main bearings.
1. Disassemble all of the internal and external electrical wiring, fire protection (CO2)
piping and instrumentation connections from enclosure roof and vent duct areas.
(See Fig. 4).
Note: On older enclosures, the lube oil feed and drain piping will have to be
disassembled so that the complete enclosure can be removed.
2. Disassemble and remove the air inlet and air discharge vent duct–rain hood
assemblies. (See Figs. 5 and 6, Detail A-A).
Note: Do not remove the damper assemblies from the enclosure roof.

Load Gear Disassembly and Alignment Readings
Remove the turbine load coupling. Then remove the generator coupling bolts and jack
generator coupling apart. When the coupling is separated jack the generator rotor aft
(toward the collector end) 0.750 inches. (See Fig. 8).
Note: Detailed instructions covering the removal of the couplings are provided in EM
5316–MS 61B Load Coupling Installation, EM 5315–Installation Procedure for
MS 6001B Gas Turbine-Generator Unit, and ML 0411–Field Alignment
Instructions.
Generator Coupling Readings
1. Remove the lube oil seal from the load (bull) gear shaft (generator end), then jack
the shaft upward enough to insert the factory supplied alignment centering ring.
(See Figs. 9 and 10).
WARNING: The centering ring must be removed after alignment is complete and
prior to turbine operation.
Note: The centering ring is supplied by the vendor and turned over to the customer at
the end of the installation phase. It is required for all generator alignment work.
2. Assemble a dial indicator strap chain around the bull gear shaft hub (generator end),
then attach two (2) dial indicators to the chain mount, and measure the generator
coupling face and rim readings. (See Fig. 11).
3. Assemble a dial indicator on the load gear (generator end), and measure the float of
the bull gear shaft to obtain a correct face reading. (See Fig. 11).
4. Install a shaft clamp fixture around the pinion gear shaft (turbine end) where it exits
the gear case. Leave a gap of approximately 0.002 inches between gear case and
clamp. (See Fig. 12).
5. Install a shaft clamp fixture around the bull gear shaft (generator end) where it exits
the gear case. Leave a gap of approximately 0.002 inches between gear case and
clamp. These fixtures will help control most of the gear float during rotation. (See
Fig. 12).
Note: These clamp fixtures should have been fabricated on-site during the installation
phase for the initial alignment of the gas turbine and generator to the load gear.
These special tools are normally turned over to the customer at the end of the
installation.

Load Gear Disassembly
The following is the recommended method of disassembling the MS 61B load gear to

INTRODUCTION
This instruction outlines the field engineering procedures to be follow when installing the Gas
Turbine 125 Volt Battery System in "FA" and advanced "H" series gas turbines.
These instructions also provide general instructions for battery system installation for the MS
3001, MS 5001, MS 5002, MS 6001, (and MS 7001, MS 9001 three-bearing set) Gas Turbine
units. (Consult the manufacturer's battery system specific instructions for installation details on
these units).
The installation procedures provided in this article cover the arrival on site, unpacking,
inspection, rigging, storage rack assembly, installation and startup of C&D (wet 1.250 specific
gravity calcium alloyed lead acid battery systems) installed into storage racks.
The battery system location is in the (PEECC) Packaged Electrical Electronic Control Center
(MLI A059) for most "FA" series gas turbines. Batteries supplied for "H" class units, or single
shaft 7001FA and 9001FA STAG units are installed in the plant battery room. (See Battery
Room Equipment).

GENERAL INFORMATION
The applicable vendor Service Instructions will normally be found in the GE Service Manual

Station auxiliaries and services consist of power distribution components used to provide
auxiliary power for starting and operating the gas turbine, compartment lighting, heating
and cooling requirements, DC emergency power and standby power needs.

During normal gas turbine operation, control and power needs are furnished by the turbine
driven load generator using the equipment described. At the time of initial startup and
during shutdown periods, standby AC power from some other source (customer supplied)
is required to maintain the gas turbine in a state of readiness.
Standby AC power is required to insure the immediate startup capability of particular
turbine equipment and related control systems when the start signal is given. Standby
power is required for the following functions:
1. Heating and circulating turbine lube oil at low ambient temperatures to maintain
proper oil viscosity.
2. Control panel heating.
3. Generator space heating.
4. Compartment heating.
5. Battery charging.
6. Exhaust frame blower motors.
7. Operation of control compartment air conditioners during periods of high ambient
temperatures to keep electrical equipment insulation within design limits.
SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
WARNING: Shock hazards are present — DO NOT TOUCH uninsulated battery,
connectors or terminals.
WARNING: Gas produced by these batteries can be explosive. Protect eyes
when working around battery. Provide adequate ventilation so that
hydrogen gas accumulations in the battery areas do not exceed two
(2) percent. DO NOT SMOKE, USE OPEN FLAME or CREATE
SPARKS near battery.
WARNING: These batteries contain sulfuric acid which can cause severe burns.
In case of skin contact with Electrolyte, immediately remove
contaminated clothing and flush affected areas thoroughly with
water. If eye contact has occurred, flush for a minimum of 15
minutes with large amounts of running water and seek immediate
medical attention.

All appropriate persons should be made aware of these safety warnings. Eye wash facilities
must be immediately available. As a minimum, at least one quart of potable water in a plastic

Unpacking and Handling
Large single cell and multicell monobloc batteries are packed in individual cartons and
strapped to wooden pallets for shipping. (See Fig. 2). Remove the straps and carefully lift
off the cartons for access to lifting slots in the bottom support pieces. (See Fig. 4).
Always lift cells from the bottom. Never lift cells by the posts. A lifting sling and spreader
are packed in the accompanying accessories box. Slip the lifting sling under the cell, then
install the spreader block on top of the cell. Use the loops in the sling to hoist the cell.
(See Fig. 5).
Note: Lifting sling loops must be crossed or held together above the spreader block,
(see Fig. 5), before lifting a battery unit (4-cell jar) to prevent the jar from tipping
and/or falling from the sling before placement on the rack.
Pre-Installation Procedures
At the first opportunity, check the electrolyte level in each cell. It should be between the
“high” and “low” level lines on the container. If the level is more than 1/2 inch below the
“high” mark, make no water additions until the cells have been on a "float" charge
for one week. (Contact the local C&D agent when this condition exists). Fill cells with a
low level to the same level as the other cells in the battery using electrolyte taken from
cells with a high level.
Accessories Package
Check the contents of the Accessories Package against the enclosed packing list to
confirm that all connecting hardware, terminal plates (if ordered), and cables have been
received. Place accessories in a safe place from which they can be easily retrieved when
needed. Record shortages and contact the local C&D agent, as required.

Battery Installation
Review the Battery Arrangement Outline drawing (MLI 1207) and note the weight of a
single jar (4-cell unit). The outline drawing indicates which battery type is applicable via
the Group number (G001 or G002).
Each of the 14 jars must be lifted over the 15 inch channel and placed on the battery rack.
(Figs. 8, 9 and 10). A lifting device (such as a counter balance lift, floor crane or engine
hoist) capable of reaching into the battery compartment is recommended. (Figs. 11 and
12).
Note: The number of battery jars will vary according to the size of the gas turbine unit,
and the whether the battery system is sized for one or two units.
To facilitate exact positioning of cell jars, lubricate the top surface of the rubber mat with
potable water. (See Figs. 13, 14, 15 and 16).
Note: Do not use grease, oil, solvents or any other substance which will damage or
destroy the battery.
Arrangement of Cells
In tiered arrangements, install the first cells on the bottom tier of the rack to provide
stability. In stepped arrangements, it may be more convenient to install the first cells on
the top step of the rack rather than on the bottom step. This will avoid moving subsequent
cells over those already placed.
Work from the center of the rack out towards both ends. Maintain a 1/2 inch space
between cells. Arrange cells on the rack so that the positive post (terminal) of the next cell
can be connected to the negative post (terminal) of the next cell. Cell post polarity is
marked with symbols molded on the cover. A plus sign (+) denotes the positive post and a
minus sign (-) the negative post.
When a rack drawing showing cell arrangement is supplied with the battery, be sure to
follow it for optimum cabling efficiency. Improper cell arrangement will result in some
cables being too long and some not being long enough.
Install tie rods (if required), to the battery rack. The tightening of tie rods must not apply
side rail pressure to the cells. Nuts used with tie rods should only be tightened to about 3-
5 ft. lbs. torque. To test this installation, an index card should be inserted between the side
rails and cell container. (See Figs. 7 and 17).

Numbering of Cells
For ease of identification, all cells of a battery should be numbered. Plastic peel-and-stick
numbers are furnished in the Accessories Package. The common practice is to start with
“1” at the positive terminal of the battery and follow the electrical circuit with succeeding
numbering. For a neat installation, first mark proposed number locations on cell jars with
chalk. Then, remove plastic backing and firmly press each number into position. Be
careful not to scratch the plastic jar.
Note: Do not use solvents to remove the original chalk mark.
Flame Arresters
All C&D standby cells use flame arresters. On small cells they are factory installed. On
large cells they are shipped separately and field installed. The large cells are shipped with
orange colored vent plugs which must be removed and discarded before installing the
flame arresters.

WARNING: Dry-charged cells must be stored with orange vent caps and plastic
film in place until ready for activation.
CAUTION: Be sure flame arresters are installed before making battery
connections.
As Received Readings
Create a report form labeled “As Received Battery Readings”. Show date, turbine number,
user customer name, site name, site location and Design Memo (DM) number in the
heading. See Appendix A, Fig. A-1).
Select a cell and designate as the pilot cell. The pilot cell, selected for the purpose of the
initial charge, is a temporary pilot cell. It should be the cell with the lowest specific gravity.
If a cell voltage is less than 2.10 volts, or the specific gravity (corrected to 77 degrees F) is
less than 1.235, contact Gas Turbine Design Engineering.
Battery Connections
Install the intercell connections and connect the battery to the battery charger(s). Refer to
C&D Manual 12-800 Installing Cells section for the procedure.
Verify that the AC supply circuit breaker for each charger is open, and that the DC output
circuit breaker for each charger is open before making any connections. (See Fig. 18).
Note: Do not connect the battery charger to the AC source (MCC) at this time.

Initial Charge
With the battery charger AC supply circuit breaker open, set the charger to “Float”, then
close the battery charger DC circuit breaker. The charger DC voltmeter should indicate
the battery voltage.
Close the battery charger AC circuit breaker. (The charger DC output current will build up
gradually). If redundant chargers are supplied, repeat this step for the second charger.
Monitor the temperature of the electrolyte in the pilot cell. A thermometer should be held in
the electrolyte for at least two minutes before taking the reading. To take temperature
readings remove flame arrester cover, and insert the alcohol-type thermometer supplied
with battery system.
Cell temperatures higher than 110 degrees F are not permissible except during the last
three hours of initial charge. At no time shall the electrolyte temperature exceed 120
degrees F. If it is apparent that the next reading will exceed these limits, interrupt the
charge and allow the electrolyte to cool to about 95 degrees F before resuming the
charge.
When the pilot cell voltage is greater than 2.18 volts, set the charger to “Equalize”. If there
are two chargers. Repeat for each charger. (See notes under Charger Settings).
Guard against electrolyte overflow. If it should become necessary to remove electrolyte to
prevent overflowing, record removals and retain the electrolyte for possible reuse.

Charger Settings
Check the battery charger(s) float, equalize settings and adjust if necessary. If redundant
chargers are supplied, disconnect the charger not being checked. See C&D Publication
RS-759 (ARE Series Single-Phase Input), or other applicable publication for complete
information.
With the battery on float charge and the charger not in the current limit mode, the battery
voltage measured at the battery terminals should be 129 +/- 0.5 Volts DC.
With the battery on equalize charge and the charger not in the current limit mode, the
battery voltage measured at the battery terminals should be 135 +/- 0.5 Volts DC.
Note: When redundant chargers with load sharing are provided, both chargers must
be set to “Float” (or both set to “Equalize”) charge while both chargers are
operating and connected to the battery.
To switch from float operation to equalize operation: Open the AC supply circuit
breaker of the redundant charger and set both chargers to "Equalize” before re-
closing the AC supply breaker of the redundant charger.
Initial Charger Readings
When the pilot cell voltage reaches 2.4 +/- 0.02 volts, set the charger to “Float”. (When
there are two chargers. (See notes under Charger Settings).
Create a report labeled “Initial Charger Battery Readings”. Show date, turbine number,
user customer name, site name, site location and Design Memo (DM) number in the
heading. (See Appendix A, Fig. A-2).
For each of the 56 cells (typical for the 7F series Gas Turbines), record voltage (+/- 0.005
V), electrolyte temperature (+/- 0.5 degrees F), electrolyte level (inches above low level
mark (+/- 1/32 inch), and specific gravity (per the Measuring Specific Gravity section of the
C&D Service Manual). Remove the flame arrester cover to measure temperature and to
return electrolyte to the cells. Use an alcohol-type thermometer supplied with the batteries
to measure cell temperature.
The report should include notes regarding any assumptions or conditions which might
effect the readings. Place a copy of the report in the charger cabinet, and send another
copy to the Customer and GE Field Office.

Equalizing
The battery requires an “Equalizing” charge if it receives a deep discharge such that the
pilot cell voltage is below 2.18 volts with the battery on float charge.
Disconnect all DC loads (especially the turbine control panel) before setting the charger to
“Equalize“. If there are two chargers, see the notes under Charger Settings.
As-Commissioned Readings
When the turbine installation and startup/commissioning is complete, a third set of battery
readings should be taken. The report form should be similar to the initial charge readings
form. See Appendix A, Fig. A-3).
Battery Room Equipment ("H" Class Advanced Gas Turbines)
Pallets of batteries will be shipped to the job site as MSD Equipment. The 125V batteries
will be installed into metal racks located in the Turbine Building on the Ground Floor under
the control room. Installer will be responsible for assembling the metal racks, installing all
of the batteries, installing the battery chargers, distribution panel, battery cables and
wiring and all other battery room equipment. Refer to DN 523 (MS9001H Advanced Gas
Turbine Installation Guide). See Figs. 19 and 20.

INTRODUCTION
This article outlines instructions for the use of a new field alignment tool currently in use on
MS7001FA and MS9001FA (single and two shaft) installations. Use of this tool is also
recommended on future MS9001H and MS7001H single-shaft gas turbine installations.
These guidelines apply to a typical centerline installation, and do not supersede any factory
instructions.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
In all cases, the Health, Safety and Environmental Manual (HSEM) will be the document
followed on the job site during installation of this equipment.
Safety, health and environmental protection must be an integral part of all department business
operations, including design, construction and start-up. Every reasonable effort will be made to
create and maintain a safe and healthful work environment.
REFERENCE DOCUMENTS
No. Description
MLI 0410 Instructions, Alignment – Factory
MLI 0411 Instructions, Alignment – Field Basic
DESIGN INFORMATION
The traditional field alignment method for gas turbines, load gears and generators has been to
attach as set 0 to 1.000 inch dial indicators to take rim and face measurement readings on the
coupling hubs while turning one of the rotors.
Although this method is practical for aligning smaller turbines, the larger FA and H Class units
require the alignment to be performed earlier in the installation sequence (before assembling
the lube oil and lift oil piping).
The method described in this article has been field proven and is recommended for alignment of
MS7001FA and MS9001FA gas turbines. Because these units have 50 and 60 ton rotors, a
new method is required to align the packages without having to turn the rotors. The concept of
using a straight-edge alignment bar was derived from similar methods used by millwrights in the
field for many years.

ALIGNMENT METHOD
This alignment procedure must be performed at a point in the installation before the lube oil
piping, lift oil piping, turning gear, and wiring have been installed.
For MS7001FA, MS7001H, MS9001FA and MS9001H Single-Shaft Installations:
1. Move the gas turbine into fine rough alignment using a straight-edge across the load
coupling and HP/IP rotor hub. Proceed to Step 2.
For MS7001FA and MS9001FA Simple Cycle or Two-Shaft Installations:
1. Move the generators into fine alignment using a straight-edge across the load
coupling and generator hub. Proceed to Step 2.
2. Use a "C" clamp to attach the alignment bar fixture (Figure 1) to the turbine load
coupling flange OD at the 12, 3, 6 and 9 o’clock positions. Take a set of rim
readings at each position (see Figure 2).
3. Use a depth gauge (Figure 3) to make a tightness check of the bar fixture to the
coupling flange through a hole drilled in the fixture. (Subtract the thickness of the
fixture from the measurement.)
4. Move the depth gauge to the HP/IP rotor hub or generator end of the bar fixture and
take the relative measurement through a hole drilled in the fixture (Figure 4).
(Subtract the thickness of the fixture from the measurement for the rim reading at
each position.)
5. Take face readings at the 12, 3, 6 and 9 o’clock positions using Adjustable Sliding
Parallels and a 0 to1.000 inch Micrometer (see Figure 5).
Note: When final alignment has been reached on single-shaft turbine installations, the
load coupling-HP/IP steam turbine spacer piece will be assembled. Refer to MLI
0411 for the procedure.
TOOL VARIATIONS
A variation of the alignment bar has been made and used during installation of a MS7001FA
Gas Turbine at FP & L and Tampa Electric with the same measurement accuracy. See Figure 6
and Figure 7.

INTRODUCTION
This document outlines basic procedures for installing the MS7001F/MS7001FA Gas Turbine
Load Coupling using the Tension Stud and Nut Tooling provided by Riverhawk Company.
Specific information for installing these bolts on other turbine models can be found at the end of
this document in Exhibit "A", Sections 1 through 4. These guidelines apply to a typical
centerline installation, and do not supersede any factory instructions.
EQUIPMENT DESIGN
The Gas Turbine Load Coupling is designed to be installed in the field after the turbine has been
set down on the foundation, leveled, aligned to foundation centerlines, and locked into place. A
set of coupling bolts must be assembled to the load coupling–turbine end.
The coupling will then be used as an alignment fixture to align the generator to the turbine.
When final alignment is completed, the set of coupling bolts will be assembled to the coupling
on the generator end.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
In all cases, the Health, Safety and Environmental Manual (HSEM) will be the document
followed on the job site during installation of this equipment.
Safety, health, and environmental protection must be an integral part of all department business
operations, including design, construction and start-up. Every reasonable effort will be made to
create and maintain a safe and healthful work environment at each customer site.

1.0 GENERAL INFORMATION
This document describes the procedure to be used when installing studs and nuts (supplied by
Riverhawk Company) in the flanges at the turbine/coupling end and the coupling/generator end
connections. This hardware tooling is depicted on drawings included throughout this document.
2.0 ASSEMBLY PROCEDURE
2.1 Machine Preparation
The flanges to be tensioned must be fully closed prior to positioning the studs in the
flanges, and there must be provision to turn the turbine and generator shafts. It will also
be advantageous to remove as many obstructions as possible from the flange area (such
as speed probes and conduit).
2.2 Hardware – Balance
• Hardware is supplied as weight-balanced sets.
• Studs and Nuts are interchangeable only within sets.
• Do not mix different sets together.
• Retain the weight certification supplied with each set for the purchase of spares.
2.3 Tensioner – Care and Handling
• When not in use, the tensioner must be maintained in a clean environment. All
caps, plugs for hydraulic openings, and fittings must be in place.
• When in use, the tensioner must be protected from sand and grit.
• For long term storage – coat the tensioner with oil, return to its original container,
and seal container to protect from moisture.
• For shipment, coat the tensioner with oil and ship in its original container.

3.0 HARDWARE PREPARATION
3.1 Nut Preparation
• For new installations, the nuts should arrive sealed from the factory with no need for
extensive cleaning.
• Nuts that have been used in a previous installation will require cleaning. Clean the
nuts with a wire brush and a petroleum based solvent to remove any foreign
material on the external surfaces and threads.
• If the previous installation employed a thread locking compound (which will be
visible as a grayish-green residue), remove as much of this compound as possible.
Note: Do not apply lubricants to the threads.
• Finish cleaning the nuts by rinsing in a volatile solvent (such as acetone) and allow
to dry.
3.2 Stud Preparation
• For new installations , the studs should arrive sealed from the factory with no need
for extensive cleaning.

3.3 Stud Length Measurement
Measure and record the initial lengths of the studs. Following the recommendations
below will improve the results.
• Plan to start and finish the flange in the same day.
• Studs and flange must be at equal temperature.
• Number each stud with a marker.
• Mark the measurement location on the stud end with a permanent marker.
• Measure each stud to nearest 0.001 inch.
• Record each measurement on the supplied charts.
• Do not expose the measuring instruments to the sun for any length of time.

This is also important for proper assembly of the windage plates. Refer to Section 11.0.
Hand tighten the assembly to a snug fit. See Figures 3 and 4 for a view of studs in flange prior

5.0 ASSEMBLING HYDRAULIC TENSIONER EQUIPMENT
5.1 Kit Assembly
Assemble the hydraulic pump with its hose to the puller tool and bleed the system of air
per the following instructions. Figure 5 shows hose connected to tensioner manifold.
5.1.1 Fittings
Ensure that both the male and female parts are clean and free of debris (see Figure
6 for fitting configuration). Hold female part securely when tightening to prevent
damage to adjacent tubing. If fitting leaks, retighten as needed. If leaking
continues, disassemble and check for scratches or debris on the seating conical
surfaces. Clean as necessary. Replace the plastic caps when finished with tooling.
5.2 Pump
The pump kit is filled with hydraulic oil when shipped, and the pump reservoir cap sealed
for containment. To prevent oil spillage, keep cap closed when not in use, or during
storage and shipping. Lost oil should be replaced with Enerpac Hydraulic Oil, ISO 32.
Mineral oil may be substituted if necessary.
5.3 Bleeding the Hydraulic System
Bleeding air from the hydraulic system must be performed before stud tensioning begins.
Follow the tensioner assembly instructions in Section 6.0.
The tensioner has four ports (see Figure 7); one for pressurizing, two for bleeding the
system, and one for pressure relief. To facilitate bleeding, start by mounting the tensioner
at either the 3 o’clock or 9 o’clock stud position, depending on which will critically place
the bleed ports in their uppermost position. In addition, ensure that the pump is always
situated below the tensioner assembly.
The puller tool is equipped with 5/8 in. Hex cone stem bleeder fittings installed in the
bleeder ports. With these two loosened simultaneously, stroke the pump repeatedly until
the streams of oil exiting the tool from each port are free of air. Retighten the fittings.
Note: The hose is stiff. Use of this tooling can be simplified by temporarily mounting
the puller tool on one stud prior to final tightening of the fittings. This will reduce
the tendency for the fittings to loosen during use.

6.0 ASSEMBLY OF TENSIONER ON STUD
Refer to the Tensioner Assembly drawing and Figure 7 for views of tensioner to flange
mounting. All tensioning is to be performed on the coupling side of the flange connection.
Note: The HT–0342 is supplied with two adapter feet and two spanner rings (the feet are
marked “turbine” and “generator”). Mount the appropriate foot before attempting to
use the tensioner.
6.1 The following features should make stud tensioning safe and easy.
• The safety cage is integral (bolted) to the puller.
• The hydraulic piston is spring-loaded to retract.
• The two-piece puller screw requires the operator to tighten the puller screw into the
stud.
6.2 Assemble as follows.
1. Place the spanner ring on the cylindrical nut. Ensure that the puller nut is loose
at the start of each assembly.
2. Place and hold the tensioner assembly over the end of the stud to be tightened.
(See Figures 5, 8 and 9.)
3. Slide the puller screw into the tapered thread of the stud and hand tighten. Ensure
assembly is not crossthreaded.
4. Hold the stud steady with a 1/2 in. hex key wrench, and lightly tighten the puller
screw into the thread with a wrench.
5. Turn the puller nut until it seats snuggly, then back off 2 flats. This is particularly
important for removal because the stud shortens during disassembly and the
tensioner may bind.
6. At this point the Tensioner Assembly MUST BE FREE TO ROTATE. The puller
screw must be tight in the stud and the puller nut must be backed off 2 flats.

7.0 STUD PULLING AND TENSIONING
The studs are to be tensioned in two steps (once at approximately 50% pressure and once at
final pressure). Follow the sequence for tensioning each flange joint as defined on the data
sheets at the end of this instruction.
Note: Before inserting the puller screw into the tapered thread of the stud, carefully clean
both the male and female threads and apply a high pressure lubricant (such as “Never
Seize”) to the male taper. This will help ease assembly and ensure positive mating of
the threads before tightening.
WARNING: The safety cage MUST be in place. Keep hands out of
designated areas at all times when the puller tool is pressurized
to prevent personal injury.
7.1 Tensioning at 50% Pressure
After the tensioner is properly installed, apply hydraulic pressure to the tool. Bring the
pressure to the 50% level in accordance with the following table.
MS7001F/MS7001FA Gas Turbines
Flange Stud Diameter 50% Pressure
Turbine/Coupling 2.283 in. 9,000 psi
Coupling/Generator 2.784 in. 10,000 psi
7.1.1 Turn the cylindrical nut using the spanner ring and pin (as depicted in Figure 7)
until it bottoms out on the flange.
7.2 Puller Tool Removal
Remove the puller tool as follows.
1. Release the puller tool pressure by opening the valve on the pump. Leave the valve
open.
2. Using a wrench, unscrew the puller screw.
3. Tap the wrench with a hammer if necessary to help loosen the puller screw.
4. Move the tool to the next stud/nut assembly to be tensioned, following the
sequence/pattern as defined on the supplied data sheets.

8.0 RETENSIONING
Excessive stretch variation or low stretch values can be corrected by retensioning all or selected

9.0 THREAD LOCKING
Once pulling and tensioning is complete, all stud nuts must be locked in position. Two methods
of thread locking may be encountered in the field. Early versions of the hardware entails a liquid
thread-locking compound, while later configurations employ a mechanical locking feature. Each
method is described in detail in Sections 9.1 and 9.2.
9.1 Thread Locking Using a Liquid Locking Compound
These nuts have no visible locking feature. Apply the specified number of drops (see
following table) of thread locking compound (Permatex Industrial “After Lock” No. 81794,
included with each set of hardware from the factory) to each end of the stud at the
stud/nut interfaces follows.
1. Apply the drops to the face of the nut at the top of the assembly, allowing material to
run down onto the stud threads.
2. An alternate method of applying the thread-locking compound is to use a short (2 to
3 in.) length of wire. Place one end of the wire at the top of the nut/stud interface
with the wire held at a 45 degree angle, and apply the liquid to the wire so that it
runs along the wire into the threads.

The procedures for removing nuts that have been locked with liquid locking compound and
those with the mechanical locking feature are described in Sections 10.1 and 10.2, respectively.
10.1 Removal of Assemblies with Liquid Locking Compound
For assemblies that have been locked with the liquid locking compound, removal is
performed as follows.
1. Using a wire brush and shop air, clean the internal tapered thread of the stud to
remove any debris and deposits that may have accumulated during service.
2. Install the appropriate puller tool to the stud as described in Section 6.0.
3. Apply hydraulic pressure per the following table and, using reasonable force, loosen
the nut using the spanner/pin wrench (as shown in Figure 7).
4. If the nut cannot be loosened, release the pressure and repeat the procedure.

15.0 ASSEMBLY OF TENSIONER ON STUD
Two types of Tensioner Kits will be encountered in the field. The two types are easily identified
by their particular safety cages. One cage is separate from the puller tool while the other is
internal. Other design differences and operational characteristics are defined in the following
Sections. The two assemblies are depicted in Figures 17 and 18.
All tensioning (pulling) is to be performed from the tapered thread end of the stud with
orientation of the stud to the flange as shown in Figures 19, 20 and 21.
15.1 Assembly of Tensioning Kit with Separate Safety Cage
Refer to Tensioner Assembly drawing and Figure 18 for mounting tensioner to flange.
Assemble as follows.
1. Open the hydraulic return valve on the pump to allow hydraulic fluid to be pushed
back from the puller tool into the reservoir as the puller tool is tightened.
2. Place the spanner ring on the puller side nut.
3. Place and hold the puller tool over the end to be tightened.
4. Insert the puller screw through the puller tool and into the tapered thread end of the
stud. Hand tighten.
CAUTION: Ensure assembly is not cross threaded.
5. Tighten the puller screw using an open-end wrench and spanner or Allen wrench,
depending upon hardware configuration, on the opposite end of the stud. (DO NOT
WRENCH THE NUT.)
6. At this point the puller screw must be tight in the stud and the tensioner assembly
must be free to rotate.
7. If the puller tool is not free to rotate when the puller screw is tight, then either (1) the
piston is not fully retracted, or (2) the stud is not properly positioned in the flange.

(3) Tighten the puller screw side nut to take up the slack.
(4) Retighten the puller screw and check for looseness of tool.

Refer to Tensioner Assembly drawing and Figure 18 for mounting tensioner to flange.
Mount as follows.
1. Open the hydraulic return valve on the pump to allow hydraulic fluid to be pushed
back from the puller tool into the pump reservoir.
2. Place the spanner ring on the puller side of the cylindrical nut.
3. Place and hold the puller tool over the end to be tightened.
4. Insert the puller screw through the puller tool into the tapered thread of the stud and
tighten.
CAUTION: Ensure assembly is not cross threaded.
5. Tighten the puller screw using Allen wrenches. Do not wrench the Hex nut opposite
the puller tool.
6. Install the puller nut until it seats snuggly on the piston, then back off 2 flats. This is
particularly important for removal because the stud shortens during disassembly
and the tensioner may bind.
7. At this point the Tensioner assembly must be free to rotate. The puller screw is
tight in the stud and the puller nut has been backed off two flats.

INTRODUCTION
This article provides detailed operating instructions for the ITH Stud Tensioning Equipment used
to install and remove tensioned casing fasteners. This method applies to MS7001FA gas
turbines shipped after September 2000 with tensioned casing fasteners. The tensioning
equipment is distributed by ITH Engineering, Inc. for use with tensioned casing studs and nuts
supplied by GE.
EQUIPMENT DESIGN INFORMATION
Clamping force on a flange is achieved by tightening the stud or nut until the stud stretches a
given length. Standard torqued casing fasteners are normally tightened and loosened by
twisting a nut on the stud. This method can result in thread galling, stuck fasteners, and
damage to casing flange counterbores. GE Gas Turbines has adopted a hydraulically stretched
(tensioned) fastener system for use on selected F-Class compressor, turbine and exhaust
casing fasteners. Hydraulically stretched fasteners are designed to minimize galling and
disassembly problems by tensioning without twisting the nut or stud. Instead, a hydraulic
cylinder assembly engages one end of the stud and hydraulic pressure is applied against the
flange to stretch (or tension) the stud. With the stud stretched, the nut is turned down tight
against the flange. Once the nut is tight, the pressure is released. The stud remains stretched
and held in tension by the nuts, exerting a predetermined clamping force on the flange. For
disassembly, the stud is again tensioned, lifting the nut off the flange. The nut is then loosened
a few turns, the hydraulic pressure is released, and the nut and stud are easily removed.

Personnel safety and protection of the environment must be an integral part of all business

PREPARATION FOR ASSEMBLY
Caution: Several important preparations must be completed before performing the
actual stud tensioning procedure with the ITH Tensioning equipment. The
following preparatory steps must be performed correctly and in sequence to
ensure safe and effective operation of the stud tensioning equipment.
Because extremely powerful hydraulic forces will be created during use of this
equipment, all operating personnel must fully understand the instructions for
operating the tensioner, and become familiar with the cautions and warnings
provided to reduce the likelihood of personal injury.
1. Assembling the Stud and Nut
1. The exposed threads of the stud must be cleaned before installing the
tensioning equipment. Clean the threads with a wire wheel or brush and inspect
them for damage. Damaged threads must be repaired before tensioning. Apply
an anti-seize compound (see Standard Practices for recommended types) to the
threads of the stud(s) to be tensioned. Each stud has a “top” (or tensioned) end,
where the tensioner is installed, and a “bottom” (or non-tensioned) end, which
has an inverted hex used to prevent the stud from rotating during installation.
Using the special Height-Adjustment socket, assemble the tensioning nut onto
the top of the stud (see Figures 5 and 6). Turn the nut on the stud until the end
of the stud lines up with the top of the cutout in the Height-Adjustment socket,
and the bottom of the socket lines up with the bottom of the nut (see Figure 7).
This establishes the correct amount of thread exposed above the nut needed to
attach the Tensioning Cylinder. Assemble the stud and nut in the turbine flange.
Assemble another nut onto the bottom of the stud, and run the nut up against
the flange hand-tight.

2. On the top (tensioned) end of the stud, measure the length of exposed thread
above the nut to ensure that there is sufficient thread exposed to operate the
Tensioning Cylinder. Establishing the correct amount of exposed thread is
important because the Tensioning Cylinder must be fully threaded onto the stud
in order to hold it securely while tensioning. To measure, set either the Socket
or the Tensioner Support on the exposed surface of the nut on the tensioned
end of the stud. See Figures 8, 9 and 10. If the end of the exposed thread falls
between the red grooves on the Socket or the Tensioner Support, then the
correct amount of thread is exposed for tensioning. Adjust the nut as needed to
obtain correct thread length. When correct thread length has been verified,
tighten the nut against the flange. Lightly impacting the nut at this point will help
prevent the stud from rotating when attaching the Tensioning Cylinder. After
tightening, re-verify that the length of exposed thread still falls between the red
grooves on the socket or Tensioner Support.

STUD TENSIONING PROCEDURE – ASSEMBLY
To ensure personnel safety, the following precautions must be observed by all personnel during
this operation.
WARNING: During stud tensioning, failure of the stud threads or
misapplication of the Tensioner may result in the tensioning
head becoming a projectile. Personnel must stand clear during
tensioning. Except for the operator, all personnel must maintain
a distance of at least 10 feet from the equipment while
tensioning. The operator must stay clear of being directly
above or in line with the tensioning cylinder while it is
pressurized.
1. To begin tensioning, first ensure that the pump shutoff valve is closed. With the
tensioning equipment in place on the stud, start the pump and let it run until the reading
on the pressure gauge indicates the previously established setting. Then shut down the
pump. The Tensioning Cylinder is now stretching the stud so that the nut is no longer in
contact with the flange.
2. Using the ½ inch-drive ratchet on the Tensioner Support Gear Drive, rotate the Gear Drive
clockwise to tighten the nut against the flange surface. See Figure 17. Remember to
use extreme caution when performing this step. Make sure that you are not directly
above or in line with the Tensioning Cylinder while it is under pressure.
Note: Do not exceed 20 foot-pounds of torque when turning the Gear Drive. Repeated
excess torque may result in Gear Drive failure.

STUD TENSIONING PROCEDURE – DISASSEMBLY
Tensioning for disassembly is essentially the reverse of assembly. For disassembly, the stud is
again tensioned, lifting the nut off the flange. The nut is then loosened a few turns, the hydraulic
pressure is released, and the nut and stud are easily removed. The preparations required for
disassembly are also much like the preparations required for assembly.
1. Starting at the tensioned end of the stud, remove the thread protectors. It is extremely
important at this point to clean the exposed threads of the stud before installing the
tensioning equipment. Clean the threads with a wire wheel or brush and inspect them
for damage. Damaged threads must be repaired before tensioning. Also carefully
clean the counterbore around the stud and nut where the tensioner will be seated. Use a
wire brush and compressed air to completely clean the surface of paint, dirt and debris.
2. Check the length of exposed thread protruding from the nut by placing either the ITH
Socket or the Tensioner Support on the exposed surface of the nut adjacent to the
exposed thread of the stud. If the end of the exposed thread falls between the etched red
grooves on the Socket or Tensioner Support, then sufficient thread is available for
tensioning.
WARNING: If the length of exposed thread is too short and does not fall
between the red grooves, do not attempt to tension the stud.
Contact Product Service or the tool manufacturer (ITH) for
removal procedures. Attempting to tension without sufficient
thread engagement can result in the tensioner head becoming a
projectile.
3. Apply an anti-seize or light oil to the clean, exposed threads. Place the Tensioner Support
with Gear Drive onto the nut. As in the assembly procedure, ensure that the flats in the
Gear Drive inner turning sleeve are evenly aligned with the flats on the nut (Figure 12).
Failure to correctly align the flats will result in damage to the inner turning sleeve. Correct
alignment is indicated when the Tensioner Support rests flatly against the flange surface.

D. Brushless exciter.
E. Exciters constructed by Other Equipment Manufacturers (OEM's).
F. Digital exciters (the exciters that will begin appearing in the near future).
Missing from the above list, and not discussed in this article, is the rotating direct current exciter,
(DC generator), that has been employed since the earliest days of power generation. The
development of the silicon diode and silicon controlled rectifier has all but eliminated the use of
rotating DC exciters (except those in existing installations). And a number of customers are
retrofitting existing units to eliminate rotating DC exciters.
During the equipment planning stages, the customer is given an opportunity to select the type of
exciter to be used, or to present requirements that may dictate the choice of exciters. The
following are what may be expected to arrive at a jobsite, based on equipment selection.
The SCT-PPT compound system, Figure 1, has been in service, for many years on both steam
and Gas Turbine-Generators. It has a reputation of being the most reliable system ever built. It
has been replaced by the other systems, described below, but may still be furnished on request,
and for this reason is mentioned here. In terms of cost it is probably on par with the Shunt SCR
exciter (the most expensive). The major components consist of a saturating current transformer

(SCT) connected in the generator's neutral circuit; a power potential transformer (PPT),
connected to the generators output; a power bridge rectifier (with linear reactors); and a voltage
regulator with excitation controls. The SCT allows this exciter to sustain excitation on sudden
load application or on system faults.
The Potential Source (or Bus Fed) excitation system, Figure 2, is currently being furnished on
numerous installations, both steam and Gas Turbine-Generators. This exciter is the least
expensive of the GE manufactured exciters used on Gas Turbine-Generators. The major
components consist of a power potential transformer (PPT) connected in the generators output;
a power bridge rectifier; and voltage regulator including excitation controls. This type of exciter
has the disadvantage of not being able to maintain excitation during extended faults, nor being
able to quickly lower excitation through an inverting bridge rectifier.
The Shunt SCR compound system, Figure 3, is currently being furnished on installations both
steam and Gas Turbine-Generators. It is probably the most expensive system presently being
used. The major components consist of a power current transformer (PCT) connected in the
generators neutral circuit; a power potential transformer (PPT) connected to the generators
output; a power bridge rectifier (with linear reactors); and a voltage regulator with excitation
controls. The PCT allows this exciter to sustain excitation on sudden load application or on
system faults.
The Brushless Excitation System, Figure 4, is presently being furnished on Gas Turbine-
Generator installations. Its price is between the Potential Source and the Shunt SCR. The
major components are: a rotating brushless exciter, a rotating power bridge rectifier "wheel",
and a voltage regulator cabinet with excitation controls. The rotating exciter enables this system
to sustain excitation for a brief period on sudden load application or on system faults. It also
eliminates brushes and collector rings. Typically, the rotating equipment is manufactured by
Electric-Machinery, and the voltage regulator may be manufactured by GE. In terms of physical
space requirements, it is probably the most compact system.
Other equipment manufacturers (OEM's) may furnish excitation systems that would be used
with GE Gas Turbine-Generators. There is a tendency to use GE equipment, but that may not
always be the case.

Prior to the start of any installation, adjustments, or checkout; it will be necessary to review
drawings, instructions, and data for the unit. Proper preparation, with attention to detail, will
help avoid making mistakes and can save considerable time later on.
Experience has shown that it is best to obtain one complete set of excitation instruction books,
generator information, and generator data. These can be inserted in a binder, and used as a
working reference. This can be fairly time consuming as it often requires using a jobsite copying
machine, to reproduce a relatively large amount of material, taken from the turbine-generator
instruction manuals.
Gas turbine-generator drawings can become a bit "challenging", because of the numerous
interconnections and the numerous GE equipment suppliers, plus other vendor and customer
drawings on top of all this. Unfortunately, these drawings are not "gathered up" under one set
of elementary, interconnect, and connection drawings. It is easy to make a mistake, (or
encounter difficulty), at a point where different parties "tie" their equipment together. Experience
has shown it is best to obtain at least (2) complete sets of all drawings, .(3) sets are even better,
before starting work. One set of drawings will be marked up, and used to prepare "as built"
drawings; these will then be returned for revision. The second set will be marked up and
retained at the site until revised drawings are issued, and if a third set is made they may be
retained in the responsible GE office, (to handle any problems that may occur until revised
drawings are issued). Failure to retain at least one extra set of marked up drawings, upon
completion of the installation, can be "risky business". In addition to marking up the necessary
GE drawings it usually becomes necessary to mark up customer, (and sometimes other
vendor), drawings. Again, extra set of marked up drawings should be retained.

In order to perform a successful start-up, (with a minimum of problems, risk, and off line
operation), it will be necessary to test, adjust and calibrate numerous items. If the excitation
system instruction manual is followed, many of the adjustments will be made with the unit
running. Running a turbine-generator to perform adjustments, that are easily made using test
equipment, will be expensive, present a degree of risk, and delay placing the unit in operation.
Also, choosing to not verify equipment calibration and operation, (with the thought that it is
"factory tested and calibrated"), can be risky. Therefore, it is appropriate to perform as much
"non-running" calibration and test work as is practical. Even if the equipment is found properly
functioning and calibrated, the assurance that a dependable excitation system will be "going to
work", can relieve some of the pressure associated with a new unit start-up. The drawback, in
performing simulated tests. Using test equipment, will be the necessity of understanding the
excitation system and its operation; there is no instruction book procedure to completely guide
one thru such tests and calibration. The following test equipment is suggested, if it is not
available it may be rented. In comparison to the cost of operating a turbine "off line", and the
cost of delays in placing a unit in operation; test equipment rental or purchase is very
reasonable.
Typical Test Equipment Required
• Three phase Variac. Nominal 115 VAC output at 2.5 AAC. Used to simulate PT signal.
• Power Supply. 0 to 500 VDC at 1.5 ADC. Used to simulate generator field voltage.
• Single Phase Variac. Nominal 115 VAC output at 2.5 AAC.
• Single Phase Transformer. 480/240-240/120 VAC, 0.33 KVA or greater.
• Power Supply. 0 to 100 mvdc. Used to simulate generator meter shunt output, (generator
field current simulation)
• Three Digital Multimeters (DMM's), 4-1/2 digit. One meter must have frequency measuring
capability. (i.e., Fluke Model 87 or 8060A).

There is a certain "intimidation" period that seems to go with the arrival at a new jobsite. Once
associates are met, drawings, data, and instruction books are reviewed; and a physical
inspection is made, this period is ended. Plans are made and checkout can begin. Usually, a
Field Engineer experienced in excitation work is brought in to perform pre-start-up checks,
adjustments, and to be on site for start-up. Normally the equipment will be installed, and the
wiring completed, before this individual arrives. It will be necessary for the Field Engineer to
procure all drawings, data, instructions, and test equipment; if this has not previously been
done. For this reason, it is best to discuss these requirements, with the Field Engineer, in
advance of their arrival at the jobsite. This will shorten the "on site" preparation period, allowing
work to begin sooner.
It is necessary to verify connection and interconnection wiring of the controls and logic circuits.
In addition, the circuits themselves must be verified for proper operation. This can sometimes be
performed in a combined check. The checks will normally be done by the Field Engineer, with
the co-operation of any other interested parties, (i. e. Turbine Controls Specialist, user
customer, architects-engineers, etc.). The equipment will extend beyond the excitation system,
reaching into other control systems that may be furnished by other GE components or other
vendors. With good co-operation, between interested parties, it may be possible to verify
several circuits simultaneously, avoiding repeat checks. It must be remembered that this will be
"untried and unproven" equipment, going into service. Any circuit that is not verified cannot be
trusted.
The Field Engineer will normally perform adjustments and checks of the various controls, prior
to start-up. Settings should be recorded on data sheets with the data retained for both the
customer and the responsible GE office. This information will be used during future
maintenance checks. The ability to perform this work will depend entirely upon having various
pieces of test equipment available.
If thorough pre-start-up checks and adjustments are completed, very little will have to be done
during start-up. There are a number of items that will have to be attended to, but pre-start-up
checks will eliminate most of this work. On the other hand, if pre-start-up checks have not been
performed and these checks and adjustments are to be made with the turbine running; plan on
several hours of "off line", (no load), generator operation. Once again, adjustment data should
be recorded. It will also be necessary to perform "on line" URAL calibration checks, if this

will typically occur, during a start-up; and for this reason it is not unusual to work long hours with
little or no rest. Long hours, (without sleep), unexpected problems requiring immediate attention,
pressure from other parties to complete work quickly; all of this while making adjustments on
operating energized equipment simply put: do pre-start-up adjustments. Different excitation
systems have their own particular concerns, but they all have in common the start-up
verification of certain operational points. Some nominal period of "off line" operation time must
be allocated for these checks.
The excitation system is only one of the many systems that may be of concern. Often times the
Field Engineer is called upon to perform checks, adjustments, and offer start-up assistance to
other systems. If other systems are also to be included, then adequate time and assistance will
be required. Also, as with the excitation system, drawings, instructions, and data; along with test
equipment, will be needed.
Typically, protective relays are included in the generator controls. In addition the customer may
include other protective relaying, located separate from the gas turbine-generator. It is
absolutely essential that these devices function properly. The protective relays should be
verified, as to their connections and interconnections, functional operation, (that is to say they
will trip the required circuit breaker), and calibration. This work can be quite time consuming,
requires specialized equipment, and specialized knowledge. It is usually best to "farm out" the
relay testing, to people who specialize in this work, even though the Field Engineer may be able
to perform this duty. Prior to relay calibration, relay settings must be obtained from the power
system engineering group, responsible for system protection. This may be GE, the user
customer, or an architect-engineering firm.
The generator controls are usually verified by the Field Engineer. They will include metering,
and with a few exceptions, it is usually more convenient to include the metering with the
protective relay calibration and testing.
Often a main generator breaker is included as part of the generator package. It will be
necessary to verify this breaker's operation and adjustments. Should the switchgear encompass
a line-up of several breakers, then plans must be made for their checkout. It is not likely that
time will permit the Field Engineer, (who may be qualified to direct this work), will be able to
follow thru on the checkout of more than one circuit breaker.
The generator may receive pre-start-up tests and checks by a Generator Specialist. Or, it may
be up to the Field Engineer to follow thru on it's readiness for service. Data sheets should be
prepared for the various system tests; as work progresses it may be necessary to repeat some
tests.

In the process of connecting the generator, bus work and cables will suddenly become of
concern. Experience has shown that it is best to keep track of this work; this may require that
the Field Engineer divide his attention between excitation and controls work and the generator
connections. On some rare occasions, knowledgeable, caring craftsmen will be assigned to
make the generator connections. In this latter case, keeping track of the work is greatly
simplified. GE information on bus connections, cable terminations, and insulation, leaves room
for improvement.
During the installation of a turbine-generator, systems reach a stage where they will be made
operational and tested. During these tests it is often necessary to by-pass protective devices,
communications is often poor, controls are not within site of the equipment, and craftsmen will
unknowingly enter the vicinity of equipment that is about to be powered up. In the case of the
exciter, the greatest areas of concern have to do with energized equipment. During exciter tests,
unless precautions are taken, it would be possible to inadvertently power up:
• Generator brush rigging.
• Potential transformers, (PT's).
• Power potential transformers, (PPT's).
• AC and DC control circuits.
• Power bridge rectifiers.
• Bus and cables.
• Fans and heaters.
• Circuit breakers.
• And perhaps other items.
Warning signs and barrier tape should be utilized, where needed. In addition, it is advised to
stop, think., and discuss the test with associates; before "powering up". As is possible, try to set
up a method of communications with remote locations; both a dedicated radio and telephone
are highly desirable, but don't expect to be provided either one.
In addition to the personnel safety hazard, there is also the hazard of damaging equipment. This
means that planning must be made before each system test. Once again stop, think., and
discuss the test before "going to work".

A Lifted Lead & Jumper Check List should be prepared, and placed in a conspicuous location.
The check list will help ensure protection and control circuits are restored, once testing is
completed. To help minimize the possibility of equipment damage, (in control circuits), it is a
good idea to use jumpers that are fused. Jumpers that incorporate fuses can be easily
constructed and the fuse ratings can be adjusted to meet differing requirements, (a 2 ampere
fuse works quite well, in most instances).
Excitation work can present some unique challenges and opportunities. Devising test and check
methods, (and equipment), that will ensure equipment start-up with maximum reliability,
minimum risk, and reduced delay are required. Along the way there will be opportunity to
practice patience, diplomacy, forgiveness, and originality.

RECEIVING INSPECTION – GENERAL
On receipt of the turbine, generator and accessory compartment, check the factory installed
accelerometers ("hump meters") to determine whether the generator may have been humped
during shipment. These meters consist of two springs and four ball bearings in a plastic cover. If
the springs are sprung, and the balls are no longer supported by the springs, the generator
experienced a rough ride and damage may have occurred. Report this to Installation
Engineering.
SETTING MAIN PACKAGES
The sequence in which the main packages are set is often a matter of the personal preference
of the field engineer, or determined by which piece of equipment arrives on site first. This
guideline procedure has chosen a sequence which has proven satisfactory during past
installations. This procedure describes a sequence in which both the turbine and the generator
are set before the load gear is set. This procedure allows setting the generator with the rotor
shipping lock in place. Prior to setting the load gear, the generator rotor locking device will be
removed and the rotor (field) moved aft to provide sufficient clearance for setting the load gear.
The following activities are common to setting each base:
• Clean the concrete foundation of debris and dirt.
• Clean all sub-sole plates and the top surface of centerline restraining blocks.
• Protect the anchor bolt threads by removing the washers and nuts and sliding lengths of
plastic pipe over the bolt threads. (See Fig. 5).
• After each base is set, remove the plastic pipe, assemble the anchor bolt washers and
nuts, and torque the nuts. (See Table 2).
• Use a hammer to sound check for lightly loaded shim packs. (Refer to EM 1081 –
Grouting Foundation Plates).
• Use a feeler gauge to determine the percent contact and/or the number of makeup shims
needed. Adjust the shims as required (Refer to EM 5036 – Setting Sub-sole plates, for
generator shim pack preparation).
NOTE: The 6A3 or 6A6 generator typically requires an additional 0.800 inch above the
Machine Base Line of the gas turbine and load gear. (See MLI 0323 – Foundation
Interface Outline, for specific requirements).
