Preparations for Setting the Load Gear
Extreme care must be taken when setting the load gear to insure that it meets leveling
requirements:
• Ensure that the shim packs have been prepared and set on the load gear sub-sole
plates. Refer to EM 5036, MLI 1603 – Foundation Bolting arrangement, MLI 0306 –
Outline Mechanical Gas turbine and Load, and MLI 0323 – Outline, Foundation
Interface-Gas Turbine Package for Shim pack thickness calculations. (See Fig. 16).
• Verify that there are no soft shim packs, i.e., more than six (6) shims in a pack.
• Distribute the shims evenly under all mounting pads to equalize the support load
and to avoid distortion of the housing and localized high stresses.
• Remove all protective shipping covers from the load gear.
Note: The leveling requirements of the load gear sub-sole plates and shim packs are
held to a closer tolerance than other package supports. All shim packs must be
in the same plane within 0.001 inch and level within 0.003 inch/foot in all
directions.
If the turbine and generator have been set previously (as described above), the following
procedures must be carried out prior to setting the load gear due to the lack of space
between packages once the load gear is set.
• Use a solvent to remove the preservative from the shaft extensions, the exterior
machine surfaces, the coupling flange faces and the rabbets.
• Inspect the coupling bolt holes, flange faces and rabbets and smooth or remove any
nicks, burrs, or other raised surface blemishes with a stone.
• Use a micrometer to measure the load gear hub rabbit fits. Take four measurements
every 45 degrees and average to find each dimension. (See Fig. 9 – Rabbet
Interference Fit Measurement).
• See the manufacturer's recommendations for lifting and setting the load gear.
Rigging should ensure that the gear is maintained in a level position at all times.

ALIGNMENT OF MAJOR EQUIPMENT
Alignment should be accomplished with reference to MLI 0410 (Factory Alignment Instructions)
and MLI 0411 (Basic Field Alignment Instructions).
Alignment procedures for the load gear, generator, turbine and accessory base are detailed in
the following paragraphs. The overall alignment of the centerline packages (i.e., turbine,
generator, load gear and accessory gear) is accomplished without rotating either the turbine or
generator shafts. Alignment readings are obtained by mounting indicators on the load gear hubs
or accessory gear hub and sweeping the stationary turbine or generator coupling hub. In
preparation for these readings, the hub surfaces must be cleaned and inspected to insure the
coupling bolt holes, flange faces and rabbets are free from nicks, burrs or other raised surface
blemishes. (Refer to EM 5211 – MS 6001B Load Gear Field Inspection; Load Gear Disassembly
and Alignment Readings section).
Rough alignment is achieved using a straight edge to roughly align the generator to load gear
coupling. The load gear should remain in its fixed position, and the turbine and generator are
aligned to it. Prior to the start of rough alignment the bases should remain torqued to the anchor
bolts at maximum value to minimize any distortion. (See Table 2 for torque values).
Note: Feeler gages and an alignment fixture, needed for the rough alignment between the
turbine and load gear.
Initial alignment is performed with dial indicators and an alignment fixture (in a manner similar to
final alignment), but prior to installation of inlet and exhaust systems to allow easier movement
of turbine.
Final alignment of the turbine must be accomplished after the weight of the inlet duct elbow and
the exhaust duct/stack are placed on the turbine.
Load Gear Alignment Preparation Activities
1. Check the level of the load gear to ensure that it has remained at 0.000 inches, in
both axial and transverse directions.
2. Check the torque on load gear anchor bolts to ensure that it has remained at 1,000
foot-pounds.
3. Ensure that the load gear is set on shim packs with a minimum of 80 percent
contact at each hold-down point.
4. Remove the load gear shipping lock.
5. Ensure that the low-speed quill shaft centering ring (MLI 0411) is in place for final
alignment. (See Figs. 19 and 20).

Alignment of Generator to Load Gear
1. Ensure that the generator coupling flange is at the proper axial location with respect
to the centerline of the generator bearing, minus 0.750 inch (as shown in Fig. 8).
2. Inspect the coupling bolt holes, flange faces and rabbet fits, then clean, smooth or
remove any nicks, burrs, or other raised surface blemishes with a stone.

pen.

specification. (Typically 0.002 inches).

float. This reading must be added to or subtracted from the face readings. (See Fig.

8. Take a rim reading and a four-point face reading at each 90 degree turn.
9. Ensure that the indicator is returned to zero after each turn. One complete revolution
will yield a sixteen-point face runout and a four-point rim runout. (See Fig. 27 for
typical alignment specifications).

The general procedure for assembly of this coupling is first to install the two adapter
plates on the respective turbine hub and load gear hub. Next, the longer section of the
coupling is assembled to the turbine coupling hub adapter plate. Then, the shorter section
of the coupling is assembled to the (already assembled) longer section. Finally, the
coupling is made up to the load gear coupling hub adapter plate. For more specific details
on this assembly procedure, refer to the vendor drawings and notes.
1. Measure and record the length of each of the adapter plate coupling bolts. Use of a
modified dial caliper has proven beneficial in obtaining these measurements. (See
Figs. 59, 60 and 61).
2. Weigh and record (in grams) each nut and bolt assembly in order to pair up equal
weight assemblies, 180 degrees apart, to obtain optimum balance.
3. Pack both of the adapter plates in dry ice (overnight if possible) to enhance the
assembly of the interference fits at the turbine and the load gear coupling hubs.
When the adapters are sufficiently shrunk, they can be assembled to their
respective hubs. (See Fig. 62).
4. Apply a light coat of Fel-Pro C-102, or equivalent, to the bolt threads and assemble
in the adapter plate.
5. Initially torque all the bolts to 350-400 ft-lbs. (Refer to MLI 0411). Note that a
hydraulic torque wrench will be needed to torque the bolts because of a lack of
space in the area, and the turbine will have to be rotated at least 180 degrees.
NOTE: Minimize turbine rotation as much as possible since lubrication is not provided to
the bearings.
6. Stretch the bolts between 0.0095 and 0.0115 inch. (Refer to MLI 0411). About 1600
to 1640 ft-lbs of torque will be required. The turbine will need to be rotated 180
degrees again.
7. The longer section of the coupling will now be assembled to the turbine coupling
hub adapter flange. Matchmarks on these pieces must be in line.
8. Apply a thin coat of Fel-Pro to the bolt threads and, while supporting the free end of
the coupling, draw up the coupling section to the turbine adapter plate, ensuring that
the rabbet fit is properly engaged. Bolts are to be torqued to 60 ft-lbs. Support the
free end of the coupling throughout this procedure. The turbine will again have to be
rotated 180 degrees.

INTRODUCTION
The information in this instruction will help guide Field Engineers through the assembly and
installation of the three-piece Lucas Airo Space (Bendix) Load Coupling. The method described
in this article does not supersede any factory instructions.
REFERENCE DOCUMENTS

DLN-064 Generator Mechanical Outline
DLN-060 and 065 Generator Package Wiring
SPECIAL TOOLS
Special turning tools required for assembly (field fabricated) are shown in Figures 1 and 2.
THREE-PIECE LOAD COUPLING INSTALLATION
Remove the Bentley Vibration Probes and conduit from the aft side (generator end) of the
Load Gear.
The Generator Field should already be floated back toward the collector end (0.750 inch
per ML 0411 instruction), so that a measurement of 31-1/2 inches is obtained from the
generator front bearing centerpunch marks (on bearing cap or on side of bearing housing)
to the face of the generator field. See Figure 3 and Figure 4.
Shrink the rabbit fit by packing the turbine end coupling adapter plate in dry ice overnight.
The turbine rotor hub and adapter plate has a 0.004 to 0.005 inch interference fit.
Assemble the plate to the turbine rotor. Torque all bolts to specification (see MLI 0411).
Turn the load gear over and float both gear shafts aft (toward the generator) until a
measurement of 74-1/2 inches is obtained between the adapter plate bolted onto the
turbine rotor and the face of the load gear. See Figure 1 and Figure 5.
Note: Once it has been started the load gear will turn by hand, and will only float
downstream 9/16 inch from the center. (See Figure 3.)

INTRODUCTION
This Maintenance Procedure currently exists as a part of a Gas Turbine Service Manual, and is
intended to establish a consistent approach to the performance of flange-to-flange maintenance
inspections for a MS6001B gas turbine. This procedure is intended to consolidate actual field
experience and other maintenance related information normally available only from widely
diverse sources. As maintenance experience is gained on this unit, this procedure will be
supplemented with additional information and descriptions of the work to be performed. This
article currently provides inspection information for Combustion Inspection workscope. The
procedures described in the text are not intended to supersede or replace specific product
department documentation.
COMBUSTION INSPECTION
CAUTION: Before proceeding with a combustion inspection ensure that the gas turbine
electrical power is tagged-out; CO2 system is deactivated, liquid fuel system is
purged, deactivated and/or the gas supply is blanked off.
DISASSEMBLY
OPERATION 1 - PREPARE TURBINE COMPARTMENT ROOF FOR REMOVAL
1. Disconnect the blower(s) motor leads, piping flanges and tubing connections at the
topside and underside of the roof.
2. Break flanges on exhaust frame cooling piping and all tubing connections.
3. Disconnect VA14 valve electrical wiring and conduit (if applicable to unit).
4. Disconnect CO2 piping and any other piping which may interfere with roof removal.
5. Unbolt the roof from the sidewall frames.
6. Check the topside and underside to ensure roof (with blowers attached) is mechanically
free to be lifted.
OPERATION 2 - REMOVE TURBINE COMPARTMENT ROOF AND SIDE PANELS
1. Attach four eyebolts to the roof section threaded receptacles provided for lifting.
2. Rig the roof (with blower(s) attached) for lifting with a chainfall or come-along in the
rigging.

3. Lift the roof off and set on suitable cribbing.
4. Remove turbine compartment side panels to gain access to turbine compartment. Store
panels and/or doors in an upright position in a protected area.
NOTE: To gain easier access to the turbine area to remove bolting and piping, it may be
desirable to remove some of the side panel vertical support beams.
OPERATION 3 - REMOVE LIQUID FUEL LINES
1. Identify and tag each fuel line so it can be reassembled to the same combustor from
which it was removed.
2. Prior to loosening and/or removal of the tube fittings, non-destructively matchmark the nut
and fitting body. This matchmark should be different from any other existing matchmark
on these fitting parts.
Note: On the new Swagelok fittings, a stop collar is incorporated between the nut and the
fitting body. Matchmarking is not required on fittings having the stop collar. See Fig.
CI-D3.
3. Disconnect the fuel lines from the fuel check valves and from the fuel supply fittings. Hold
the fittings steady with a backup wrench to prevent twisting the fitting on the tube. See
Figs. CI-D2 and CI-D3.
CAUTION: Do not use pipe wrenches or adjustable wrenches which will result in fitting
damage.
a. Always use open-end, or tubing box wrenches.
b. Cap the open end of the fuel lines to prevent entry of dirt, insects or other
contaminants.
CAUTION: Do not use improper size caps or rags to cover pipe openings, they may be
accidentally pushed inside the tubing.
c. Where applicable, liquid fuel purge lines will have to be removed. Follow the same
general directions as stated above.
Note: When fuel purge lines are clamped to the atomizing air lines. It is advisable to leave
the clamps intact and remove both lines together.

OPERATION 4 - REMOVE ATOMIZING AIR LINES
1. Identify, tag, and nondestructively matchmark each piping pigtail with the combustion
chamber number before removing.

3. Disconnect flange at atomizing air manifold ring and remove piping. See Fig. CI-D4.
4. Clean all flange faces and cover all pipe openings. Clean all nuts and bolts and throw

CAUTION: Do not use improper size cap or rags to cover pipe openings, they may be

OPERATION 5 - REMOVE GAS FUEL LINES (If Applicable)

number before removing.
2. Disconnect flanges at fuel nozzle assemblies. See Fig. CI-D5.
CAUTION: Support the fuel gas manifold so that as fuel nozzles are disconnected, the
weight of the manifold is not on the last fuel nozzle disconnected.
3. Disconnect flanges at gas manifold, and remove piping pigtails. See Fig. CI-D5.
4. Clean all flange faces and cover all pipe openings. Clean all nuts, bolts and discard old
gaskets. Bag bolts, nuts and identify for reassembly.
OPERATION 6 - REMOVE STEAM INJECTION LINES (IF APPLICABLE)
1. Check to ensure the pigtail and manifold to the corresponding combustion casing is
matchmarked. If not matchmarked, do so.
2. Disconnect the flanges at the combustion casing cover and at the manifolds. See Fig. CI-

1. Lock out power supply to spark plugs and flame detectors to insure against any possibility

4. Unbolt the collar around flame-detector stem which prevents the turbine compartment air

5. Unbolt flame-detector flange, and remove probe from chamber. See Fig. CI-D11.
6. Disconnect spark plug leads at the spark plugs.
7. Unbolt spark plug assembly from casing flange. See Fig. CI-D12.
8. Lift spark plugs out.

matching flange surfaces. Do not reuse old gaskets.

weight prior to start of disassembly of the outer combustion
casings.

INSPECTION PROCEDURES
OPERATION 1 - PRESSURE TEST FUEL OIL AND PURGE CHECK VALVES (See Fig. CI-I1)
WARNING: Pressure testing of the fuel oil check valves requires the use of
high pressure oil or air. Use hoses, fittings and associated
equipment suitable for high pressure. Do not use faulty
equipment since its failure could cause injury. Observe safety
precautions applicable to working with high pressure gases.
1. Using distillate fuel oil, apply 75 psig in the flow direction and check for leakage. There
should be zero leakage.
2. Apply 1000 psig oil pressure against the flow direction, to each check valve to ensure
against backflow leakage, or use 80 to 100 psi air pressure while submerging the valve
under water. There should be zero leakage.
3. If leakage is observed in either direction during the leak tests, the check valve should be
replaced or repaired in the following manner:
a. Valve Disassembly, Inspection and Reassembly
1. Mount valve vertically in a vise or suitable holding fixture by clamping on the hex
of the body portion, (outlet side), taking care not to damage the threaded
connection.
2. Using a proper size box wrench on the hex of the inlet cap, (inlet side), turn the
inlet cap counterclockwise to initially loosen. The inlet cap has spring tension on
it, so carefully turn out the cap while relieving the spring tension and remove it
from the valve body.
3. Remove the body portion from the vise. Internal parts may now be tapped out by
striking the body against hand or other soft surface, or by inserting a small brass
or wooden rod into the outlet end and gently pushing on the poppet valve
assembly.
4. Check the "O" ring for cuts or cracks, check the poppet assembly for nicks, burrs
etc. and check for dirt or chips that may cause the valve not to seat properly.
5. Clean the valve body and internal parts with cleaning solvent and allow to dry.

Fuel Nozzle Reassembly
1. New parts are frequently plastic coated, be sure that all plastic material is removed before
reassembling the nozzle. Ascertain that no plastic material remains lodged on inside
surfaces.
2. Do not use Teflon tape or liquid sealant anywhere in the fuel nozzle assembly.
3. Ascertain that all gaskets are new. Never reuse an old gasket.
4. Use FEL-PRO C-102 anti-seize compound on all threaded parts.
5. During reassembly of the fuel nozzle, use the torque values specified on the fuel nozzle
assembly drawing in the Parts Lists and Drawings volume of the Service Manual.
6. Use a torque wrench with a range from zero to approximately 20 percent above the
maximum torque required for assembly. The accuracy should be within ±5 percent.
7. Hold the transition piece lightly, but firmly, in a vise, using two soft metal blocks of
sufficient width and depth to grip the hex of the transition piece housing in the vise jaws.
See Fig. CI-I3.
8. Insert the fuel nozzle pilot into the transition piece body, making sure all parts bottom
properly against their seats. See Fig. CI-I3.
9. Wipe anti seize compound lightly on the internal transition piece threads and the retainer
piece threads.
10. Screw the retainer into the transition piece. Using a straight 0.500 inch hex wrench,
socket, and torque wrench, torque the retainer to 40 ft. lbs. See Fig. CI-I3.
11. Using a suitable holding fixture, secure the fuel nozzle body in a vertical position, bore
side up.
12. Wipe anti-seize compound lightly on the external threads of the transition piece assembly
and on the corresponding threads in the fuel nozzle body.
13. Carefully install a new gasket into the fuel nozzle body, making sure that it is seated
against the retaining seat in the fuel nozzle body.

Fuel Nozzle Testing
CAUTION: The fuel nozzle must pass the following air flow, and fuel flow tests to insure
integrity of assembly and function before being returned to service or storage.
1. Fuel Nozzle Flow Check
a. The flow through the nozzle cannot be adjusted. Burrs, nicks, or dents on mating
surfaces will adversely affect flow.
b. Test for flow in accordance with the requirements on the fuel nozzle assembly
drawing in the Parts Lists and Drawings Volume of the Service Manual.
2. Fuel Nozzle Liquid Fuel Flow and Spray Pattern Check
a. Install the fuel nozzle assembly in a test fixture as illustrated in Fig. CI-I11.
b. Check for a symmetrical spray pattern of the fuel nozzle assembly.
c. Check the fuel flow through the fuel nozzle in accordance with the requirements
specified on the fuel nozzle assembly drawing in the Parts Lists and Drawings
Volume of the Service Manual.
d. Excess (rich) fuel flow indicates that the exit orifice and/or the pilot slots and holes
may be too large, or improper pilot assembly, allowing too much oil to pass by the
pilot. Low (lean) fuel flow indicates that the holes and slots in the nozzle may be
plugged or contain burrs which restrict flow.
Fuel Nozzle Storage
1. Serviceable fuel nozzles should be stored as complete assemblies in separate containers
designed to prevent damage to nozzles during storage. If the fuel nozzles are to be stored
for an indefinite time, it is recommended that they be stored in a corrosion-free
atmosphere.

5. Prior to installing the spark plug assembly to the unit, test the spark plug as follows:
reconnect the spark plug lead, with the plug out of the unit but with its body resting
against the turbine shell (or other grounded metal). Make sure the center electrode
is not grounded.
WARNING: Do not test spark plugs (ignitors) in or near an area with
explosive atmosphere.
Be careful of high voltage when testing. Energize the ignition circuit and check the
spark of the plug for approximately two (2) minutes. If heating occurs at a point
about 4 inches up from the tip, this indicates arcing between the core and ceramic
rod contact. This can be remedied by disassembly of the spark plug and cleaning of
the core electrical contact. If arcing does not occur at the tip of the electrodes,
recheck for clean electrodes and recheck the electrode gaps at 0.085 to 0.095 inch
between center and side electrodes. Gaps on either side of the center electrode
must be equal within 0.010 inch.
If the plug still does not fire properly, check voltage to the ignition transformer, and
check ignitor lead voltage by disconnecting the lead from the ignitor and arcing the
lead to ground.
Note: Be sure that the tip of the lead is within one-half inch of ground before
ignition voltage is applied.
If no arcing occurs between the tip of the lead and ground, the transformer and/or
lead are defective and should be replaced. If arcing occurs, the spark plug is faulty
and should be inspected for an open circuit, short etc.

OPERATION 10 - INSPECT AND TEST FLAME DETECTORS
Note: The flame detector tube is contained in the flame sensor subassembly. Combined with
the body and window subassembly, the two subassemblies form the ultraviolet flame
sensor. If during inspection and testing the sensor is found to be faulty, it should be
replaced as a complete assembly.
1. Clean the scanner lenses. Reconnect flame detector wiring and energize the control
panel. With power on the control panel, check that FL-1 and FL-2 indicating lights are on.
CAUTION: Reverse polarity will destroy the detector.
2. With the detector amplifier power on, verify base wiring polarity at the sensor junction box
by reading 290 VDC (minimum) across leak pair.
3. Turn power off and connect black detector lead to plus (+) and the white lead to minus (-).
4. Using a ultraviolet source at the sensor, assure that each flame detector picks up and
drops out when ultraviolet source is placed in front of the sensor and removed.
Note: A high level of ultraviolet is defined as a match or candle at a distance of less than 2
inches. The unit, however, should be capable of detecting a match or candle at
approximately 18 inches.

ring. Prior to torquing the bolts, check for proper floating seal engagement to the first
stage nozzle retaining ring slots. Torquing aft bracket bolts with floating seals out of their
slots will result in damage to seal. Torque aft bracket bolts to 75-85 lb. ft. Do not bend
lockplate tabs at this time.

lockplates from the support clamp.

9. Starting with number five (5) transition piece, check the spacing between four and five,
five and six transition pieces at the transition piece side seal slot. The spacing should be
between 0.36-0.53 inch. To align the number five (5) transition piece the aft bracket bolts

alignment is achieved on number five (5) transition piece, retorque the aft bracket bolts to
75-85 lb. ft. See Fig. CI-R11.

the compressor discharge casing. Using a carpenters square or two scales (rulers),
measure the concentricity of the transition piece to the compressor discharge casing at
four (4) points (radial outside position and every 90° from that point). If displacement does
not exceed 0.100 inch radially or circumferentially, proceed to Step 11. See Fig. CI-R12.

g. Place unit on ratchet and observe for leaks, rubs, and control deficiencies.

associated with a frame 6001B Hot Gas Path Inspection. It describes the overall work scope,
but does not detail specific methods. Its primary purpose is to provide an overview of a typical
inspection process. Design changes subsequent to the issue date of this document may not be
reflected in this guide.
This document does not purport to cover all aspects of a particular inspection. Unit-specific
details are provided in the document and drawing packages supplied with each requisition, and
all sketches and descriptions are to be considered “Typical.” This document is property of
General Electric and is considered Company Proprietary Information.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
The GI&FS Environmental Health & Safety Manual (EHSM) outlines the requirements that must
be followed on the job site during an installation or maintenance outage.
Safety, health, and protection of the environment must be an integral part of all business
operations, design, construction and start-up, and includes EHS planning prior to and during
work to anticipate and minimize hazards and incidents. Every reasonable effort must be made
to create and maintain a safe and healthy work environment at each customer site.
Where working conditions are not covered by these safety requirements and procedures, or
when a requirement or a procedure is not completely understood, obtain specific instructions or
clarification from manager, supervisor or EHS before proceeding with the work.
INTRODUCTION
This Maintenance Procedure currently exists as a part of a Gas Turbine Service Manual, and is
intended to establish a consistent approach to performing flange-to-flange maintenance
inspections for an MS6001B gas turbine. This procedure consolidates actual field experience
and other maintenance related information normally available only from widely diverse sources.
As maintenance experience is gained, this procedure will be supplemented with additional
information and descriptions of the work to be performed. This article currently provides
inspection information for Hot Gas Path Inspection workscope. The procedures described in the
text do not supersede or replace specific product department documentation.

OPERATION 2 - REMOVE EXHAUST AND INLET PLENUM ACCESS PANELS
1. On straight up exhaust configurations, unbolt the removable exhaust duct transition piece
panel on the forward side of the transition piece.
2. On side exhaust configurations remove any architectural lagging and support members
which may interfere with turbine casing removal.
Before the removable panel on the forward wall of the units exhaust plenum can
be removed, the upper section (right side looking with air flow) of the 11th stage
extraction piping and compressor bleed valve (33CB-2) must be removed.
3. Disconnect the tubing runs attached to the head of the bleed valve and the tubing runs
attached to the extraction piping at both ends. Remove the "U" bracket that supports the
actuating cylinder, loosen the slip joint clamp and unbolt the extraction line from the
compressor casing.
4. Rig to remove the piping, slip the piping out of the expansion joint and lift the piping clear
of the unit. Set the piping on suitable material to protect the valve and tubing runs. Cover
all openings on piping and compressor casing.
5. Remove the forward upper half segment clamp bars and the flex seal plates between the
exhaust hood frame and exhaust plenum.
6. Unbolt the forward exhaust plenum removable access panel. Rig to lift the panel.
The compressor bleed valve discharge pipe, insulating packs and the
compressor bleed valve diffuser box are part of this panel and should not have to
be removed.
7. Install a length of 4 inch pipe or timber and 10 ton mechanical jack across the horizontal
opening of the plenum and spread the plenum sufficiently enough to remove the access
panel. Lift panel clear of the unit.
8. Unbolt and remove the inlet plenum access door located in the lower right hand section of
the plenum, looking with air flow.

OPERATION 3 - TAKE INITIAL COMPRESSOR AND TURBINE ROTOR POSITIONING
CHECKS
Rotor positioning checks must be done with all casings bolted in place and unit supported on its
own supports.
Do not confuse clearanceometer holes and probe holes. Clearance meter holes
are too small for a depth micrometer. Use probe holes for taking tip clearances
Caution on turbine and compressor. Compressor or Turbine probe plugs may become
stuck or tight over time based upon material, temperature and torque
procedures. If difficulty occurs while removing a plug, a judgment must be
made as to whether the reading is necessary. Caution must be maintained if the
plug is to be removed by drilling. A bushing or stop block should be used to
prevent the drill bit from exceeding the required travel distance X, as seen in
HGP-D1.
1. Using random 1st stage compressor blades, take feeler clearance checks at six points:
top centerline, bottom centerline, and above and below the horizontal joint on each side.
Record clearances on Inspection Form GT7200. It may be necessary to use the hydraulic
ratchet to position a random blade tip below the probe holes for the 13th and 17th stage
compressor and 1st stage turbine for rotor positioning checks.
2. The 13th stage compressor holes (4 total) are located 7.46 inches aft from the forward
face of the compressor discharge casing forward flange.
3. The 17th stage compressor probe holes (4 total) are located 19.96 inches aft from the
forward face of the compressor discharge casing forward flange.
4. The first stage turbine probe holes (4 total) are located 27.44 inches aft from the forward
face of the turbine casing forward flange.
5. Compressor tip clearances at the 13th and 17th stages are taken by removing the plugs
located ten (10) degrees off top and bottom vertical centerline and sixteen (16) degrees
above each horizontal joint. A stamped number next to the plug counterbores indicates
the thickness of the casing from the bottom of the counterbore to the inside diameter of
the casing. Record clearances on Inspection Form GT7200.
6. Turbine casing probe holes exist (4 total) so that the turbine bucket tip clearances can be
taken on the first-stage turbine buckets. Record the turbine tip clearances on Inspection
Form GT7200. Turbine rotor tip clearance readings are taken as follows:
a. Remove plug and place an adapter into the machined counterbore of the casing.
The adapter will allow the base of the depth micrometer to rest squarely on the
casing, thereby allowing the micrometer rod to penetrate the probe hole accurately.

OPERATION 6 - REMOVE TURBINE CASING BOLTS AND UPPER HALF FIRST STAGE
NOZZLE ECCENTRIC PIN
1. Unbolt the upper half circumferential bolting between the turbine casing and exhaust
hood.
2. Unbolt the upper half circumferential bolting between the turbine casing and the
compressor discharge casing.
3. Remove the horizontal joint bolting and body-bound bolting. (Horizontal body-bound bolts
are removed by driving them upward.)
4. Mark body bound bolts for replacement in same holes.
5. Remove upper half eccentric pin near the top vertical centerline of the turbine casing.
Stamp the pin to identify it as the top eccentric pin.
OPERATION 7 - REMOVE UPPER HALF TURBINE CASING (SEE FIGURE HGP-D2)
The lifting beam, trolley hoist and spreader bar are applicable to vertical exhaust stack
configurations only. For side exhaust stack configurations use overhead crane and normal
rigging.
1. Procure the turbine casing lifting beam and trolley hoist. Install the stops on the forward
end of the lift beam and install the trolley hoist. Clamp the trolley hoist in the forward most
position on the lift beam and install the aft stops.
2. Rig to lift the beam-hoist assembly with an overhead crane. Lift the beam-hoist and guide
it into the forward opening of the exhaust duct transition piece as far as the rigging will
allow.
3. Using a chainfall or comealong mounted in the transition piece, slide and guide the lift
beam into the mounting slot(s), bolt the lift beam at the slot(s) and at the plate on the
beam to the transition piece.
4. Remove the rigging and release the clamp on the trolley hoist.
5. Attach the spreader bar to the trolley hoist hook and position the trolley over the turbine
casing.
6. Lubricate and install guide pins and jackbolts. Refer to Standard Practices, Section 2 -
Special Tools in the Service Manual.

The use of proper tools for taking clearance measurements is an important factor
in obtaining correct readings. Section 2, Standard Practices.
String tie all hand tools to the wrist to avoid loss in the turbine.
Caution
LEFT SIDE AND RIGHT SIDE (DEFINITION)
1. The left side of the machine by definition is the left hand side when the observer is facing
the compressor inlet and looking downstream (direction of air low) toward the generator
load coupling end.
ROTOR FLOAT (THRUST CLEARANCE)
1. The maximum total fore and aft movement of the rotor without distorting any of the rotor or
bearing mounts is usually 14 to 20 mils. The rotor should be against the active thrust
bearing but not loaded to deflect the bearing or casings when the indicator is read.
2. The rotor float is measured by mounting a dial indicator from the No. 1 bearing housing
and indicating on the accessory coupling hub. This can be accomplished with the
accessory coupling and guard in place. Rotor float is referenced to the No. 1 bearing
housing.
3. The rotor is moved from the load gear turbine coupling. Remove the upper half of the
load coupling guard. A small hydraulic jack and wood blocking can be placed between
the forward load gear bearing housing and the coupling flange to push the rotor forward.
The rotor will move "all-at-once" with a solid "bump." Release the jack loading before
reading the dial indicator. Reposition the jack and blocking to push the rotor aft from the
No. 2 turbine bearing housing. The rotor will "bump," release the jack and read the
indicator. Repeat three times to ensure repeatability. Record thrust clearances on
Inspection Form GT7200.
Do not jack against the exhaust plenum.
Caution
TURBINE ROTOR CLEARANCES
1. The rotor must be positioned upstream against the active thrust bearing but not loaded.
Any pressure applied in moving the rotor forward for the float check should be released at
this time.

OPERATION 9 - UNBOLT AND REMOVE TRANSITION PIECES
Transition pieces numbers 10, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9 can be removed radially outward through the
turbine casing opening. Transition pieces 4, 5 and 6 must be removed through the
corresponding compressor discharge casing opening.
1. Remove the shoulder bolt, lockplate, and aft side seal stop from between 1 and 10 and 10
and 9 transition pieces. Remove the transition piece aft side seals radially outward.
Identify the aft side seals and seal stop according to transition piece location.
2. Remove the shoulder bolt(s) and lockplate(s) that secures the number 10 transition piece
aft bracket to the first stage nozzle retaining ring. Discard the bolt(s) and lockplate(s). Do
not reuse.
3. Move the number 10 transition piece forward and away from the first stage nozzle
retaining ring to disengage the floating seals.
4. Slide the transition piece out of the forward support clamp (bullhorn) retaining slots and
remove the transition piece radially outward. Identify and tag the transition piece
according to combustion casing location.
5. Disassemble the forward mounting bracket lockplates, shoulder bolts, support clamp
(bullhorn) and forward mounting block and or shims from the number 10 position. Identify
support clamp (bullhorn) block and or shims according to location. Discard the bolts and
lockplates. Refer to Standard Practices, Section 2 for proper marking procedure.
6. Repeat Steps 1 through 5 for transition pieces numbers 1, 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9.
7. Remove the shoulder bolt, lockplate, and aft side seal stop from between 4 and 5
transition pieces. Remove the transition piece aft side seals radially outward. Identify the
aft side seals and stop according to transition piece location.
8. Disassemble the forward mounting bracket lockplates, shoulder bolts, support clamp
(bullhorn) and forward mounting block and or shims from number 4 transition piece.
Identify support clamps according to transition piece location. Discard the bolts and
lockplates.
9. Remove the aft bracket shoulder bolt(s) and lockplate(s) that secures number 4 transition
piece aft bracket to the first stage nozzle retaining ring. Discard the bolt(s) and
lockplate(s).
10. Move the number 4 transition piece forward and away from the first stage nozzle retaining
ring to disengage the floating seals. Remove the transition piece axially outward through
the compressor discharge casing opening.
11. Identify and tag the transition piece according to combustion casing location.
12. Repeat Steps 7 through 11 for transition pieces 5 and 6.

OPERATION 10 - TAKE FIRST STAGE NOZZLE RADIAL CONCENTRICITY CHECKS
Concentricity is the condition wherein the center of one symmetrical feature coincides with the
center of another. The measurement of concentricity of the first stage nozzle is the amount of
deviation of the nozzle assembly from the center of the hot gas path. Assistance from the GE
Field Service Representative is recommended when taking concentricity checks.
1. Prior to taking concentricity checks on the first stage nozzle, ensure that the bottom
eccentric pin is installed and that the lower half support ring dowel pins are assembled.
2. The first stage nozzle must be fully assembled prior to taking radial concentricity checks.
3. Take the concentricity readings as shown on Inspection Form GT9250 and Figure HGP-
D10. Record all readings on the Inspection Form. Report readings to the GE Field
Service Representative for evaluation and disposition.
The 1st stage nozzle is to be concentric with the support ring hot gas path within
a tolerance of 0.050 inch, taking into account any ellipticity in the nozzle
assembly. See alignment diagram in the Reference Drawing Section of the
Service Manual.
OPERATION 11 - REMOVE UPPER HALF FIRST STAGE NOZZLE (WITH SUPPORT PAD
AND RETAINER)
There are two types of first-stage nozzle arrangements presently in use, one type uses a
support pad seal and a seal retainer for each segment when assembled to the support ring.
The second type is known as a universal first-stage nozzle arrangement and has a tangential
support pin assembly consisting off an offset bushing, support pin, retainer and lockplate for
each segment when assembled to the support ring. Use the disassembly procedure applicable
to your unit’s configuration. See Figure HGP-D11.
1. Remove the horizontal joint bolting and clamps from first stage nozzle. Do not remove the
joint dowels. Identify horizontal clamp for left and right side.
2. Carefully lift the top half of the first stage nozzle using a chain fall. Pay special attention to
the support pad seal between nozzle and support ring. The support pad seals must slide
out of the inner support ring. See Figure HGP-D11.
3. Clean the support pad seal area, and check for and remove any burrs on edges of support
pad seal grooves and tongues.
4. Set the nozzle flat on a piece of plywood or equivalent to protect it from damage.

Nozzle Cracking
Nozzles experience several thermal gradients during starting as well as high temperatures
during loading operation. Such conditions frequently cause nozzle cracking. In fact, cracking is
expected. With certain exceptions, this cracking does not impair the efficiency or the
mechanical integrity of the nozzle. Figures HGP-I1 through HGP-I5 display typical cracking
patterns. The cracks shown are acceptable and do not require immediate repair. If uncertainty
arises in regard to any cracks, such as types not represented by Figures HGP-I1 through HGP-
I5, contact the GE Field Service Representative for disposition. Obtain specific advice prior to
making repairs when nozzle condition is considered beyond established limits.
Although to date very few cracks have been found that could impair the mechanical integrity,
cracks may still exist. The inspector should be alert for the following which may require
immediate disposition (i.e., repair or scrap).
1. Open cracks in critical areas: open cracks can permit ingestion of hot gases. An open
crack is defined as a crack sufficiently open to pass a 0.005 inch feeler gauge and having
a length of 1.0 inch or more. The critical areas are certain regions of the vane and inner
sidewalls and are shown in Figure HGP-I6.
2. Cracks that could cause part breakout: cracks whose orientation and growth rate are
such as to raise questions of the dislodgement of significant portions of the nozzle must
be evaluated. See Figures HGP-I7 and HGP-I8 for more details.
3. Continuous fillet cracks on one vane side: racks such as this can cause air-foil
separation. See Figure HGP-I8 for further details.

Nozzle Damage from Foreign Objects
Nozzles can be severely damaged by foreign objects in the gas stream. This damage can
impair the structural integrity and aerodynamic performance of the nozzle. It should be
evaluated using the following criteria.
1. All tears and breaks must be evaluated by the same criteria given above for cracks.
2. Raised metal must be blended to the adjacent surface contours.
3. Nicks and chips must not exceed 50% of the wall thickness.
4. Cooling holes must be open enough to pass a 0.050 inch wire.
Corrosion or Erosion of Nozzles
There have been no cases of severe corrosion or erosion of nozzles to date. The following
guidelines are provided in the event that such cases develop.
1. The allowable amount of vane region metal removal is 50% of wall thickness (0.100 inch).
2. Sufficient trailing edge material must be maintained to prevent nozzle cooling hole
exposure.
3. Area and harmonic checks must be performed where significant material has been
removed.
Recommendations
a. First stage nozzles should not be removed for repair except at normal hot gas path
inspection intervals unless the above guidelines have been exceeded.
b. If the nozzle is removed earlier than hot gas path inspection interval for other reasons, all
cracks, damage, etc. should be carefully mapped using proper non-destructive test
procedures and reported to the GE Field Service Representative. Do not send to repair
facility until mapping has been reviewed and specific Gas Turbine Division
recommendations are received from the GE Field Service Representative.
c. At all other times that the nozzle becomes partially or wholly accessible, the nozzle should
be inspected as completely as possible using appropriate techniques and results reported
to the GE Field Service Representative.
d. All inspections should be reported using the GT series Inspection Forms. It should be
noted that extreme care should be used to ensure accuracy. False indications can occur
when accessibility is limited. Such false indications could result in major expense and lost
time if not scrutinized and properly interpreted. Record condition of nozzles on Inspection
Forms GT9255, GT9260, GT9270, GT9295, GT9310, and GT9320.

First Stage Buckets
a. Cracks - Cracks on first stage buckets are unacceptable with one exception: radial cracks
on the bucket squealer tip less than 0.2 inch long are permissible. These cracks usually
occur as a result of Foreign Object Damage (FOD). Crack detection requires the use of
fluorescent penetrant on buckets. Zyglo ZL-22A penetrant is desirable because it will
detect tight cracks which red dye type penetrant cannot detect. Radial cracks in certain
areas of the squealer tip may be remedied by removing material. The limits are covered
the Missing Metal section.
b. Dents - Dents are permissible with the following limits.
1. The dent must not contain any cracks per the above paragraph.
2. The dent must not obstruct the diameter of, or penetrate into, a cooling air hole.
The cooling hole closest to the leading edge should pass a 0.067 inch diameter wire
or next larger standard ball to be acceptable. Holes 2 through 12 must pass a 0.050
inch diameter wire or a next larger standard ball to be acceptable. The trailing edge
hole must pass a 0.034 inch diameter wire or next larger standard ball to be
acceptable.
3. A dent must not be more than 0.090 inch deep. Therefore in areas where metal
thickness to a cooling hole is not the limiting factor, a dent may be blended to
remove resulting cracks or metal displacement, providing the 0. 090 inch limit is not
exceeded.

c. Missing Metal - Missing metal on first stage buckets occurring in the squealer portion can
be repaired by blending. Missing metal or radial cracks in the squealer portions can be
corrected within the following limits:
1. The squealer tip wall may be removed for a surface distance of 1.0 inches from the
leading edge on the suction side of the bucket. The squealer tip wall may be
removed for a surface distance of 0.50 inch from the leading edge on the pressure
side of the bucket. See Figure HGP-I11, Squealer Tip Repair Limit.
2. Missing metal, dents and blending cracks in the leading edge must not extend more
than 0.750 inch down from the top edge of the bucket. No more than a total of five
buckets may have leading edge blending below the squealer section without a
resultant loss in performance. See Figure HGP-I11, Leading Edge Repair Limits.
d. Corrosion - First stage buckets are more susceptible to damage by corrosion, erosion,
and oxidation than second or third stage buckets. This condition usually first appears on
the leading edge of the airfoil as a flattening and roughening of the surface; however, the
entire airfoil is susceptible to corrosion, erosion or oxidation attack.
Direct measurement of this wearing is difficult, if not impossible. However, general criteria
can be established. The cooling hole closest to the leading edge is approximately 0.15
inch from the leading edge, and about 0.06 inch from the airfoil suction side surface. The
corrosion pattern on the leading edge will allow a maximum of 0.088 inch corrosion before
a breakdown of the hole closest to the leading edge occurs. This breakdown appears as
a depression on the suction side surface, near the leading edge. If this condition appears
on the first stage buckets, replacement is required.
If some lesser amount of corrosion is observed, judgment is required to weigh the
possibility of a corrosion related failure against the cost of replacement of buckets at the
time of inspection. Realize that 0.088 inch of corrosion constitutes a total corrosion life.
The fraction of 0.088 inch removed is the fraction of the life used. (It is assumed that
corrosion progresses linearly with time.) Replace the buckets if total corrosion life is
predicted before the next planned inspection.

Second and Third Stage Buckets
a. Cracks - Cracks also occur in the second and third stage buckets due to foreign object
damage. These cracks usually occur at the airfoil leading edge in the outer span sections.
1. Second stage bucket cracks are repairable if located in the outer 20% of the airfoil
and up to 0.250 inch in length. See Figure HGP-I12, Second Stage Bucket Repair
Limits.
2. Third Stage bucket cracks are repairable if located in the outer (1/3) one-third of the
airfoil and up to 0.350 inch in length. See Figure HGP-I12 Third Stage Bucket
Repair Limits. These cracks can be repaired by blending the airfoil in the area of the
crack while maintaining radii at all intersection points. The leading edge radius must
also be retained in the repaired area.
b. Missing Metal - Missing material in the second and third stage buckets is acceptable if
the airfoil can be contoured to the same limits as crack repair.
c. Dents - Dents are acceptable, as long as the dent is not located in the bucket root fillet
(interface between airfoil and platform) or in the shroud fillet (interface between airfoil and
shroud).
Dents containing cracks or those located in the shroud fillet are repairable. Repairable
dents should be hand polished to remove foreign material in the area of the dent, and
fluorescent penetrant inspected for cracks. Blend smooth all dents.
d. Air-cooled second stage buckets must pass a 0.050 inch diameter wire through all four
holes from the bucket tip to beyond the platform. An additional check should be made to
insure that the passage ways through the bucket shank is open and clear.
e. Corrosion - Corrosion on second and third stage buckets to a depth of more than 0.025
inches has not been observed. Such a condition is acceptable. If a more serious
corrosion is noted, the observations should be reported to the GE Field Service
Representative.

1. Clean nozzle assembly by blasting with aluminum oxide 220 grit or finer as detailed in

tooth height. Compare this measurement to the height of the tooth on the diaphragm

OPERATION 6 - MAKE FIRST STAGE NOZZLE ELLIPTICITY CHECKS
Ellipticity is deviation from a perfect circular form toward an ellipsoidal form. Measurement of
the first stage nozzle is to determine the amount of deviation ("out-of-roundness") of the nozzle
assembly when it is measured out of the unit. Ellipticity can be measured on the first stage
nozzle since the segments are held in place by a retaining ring and are removed as an
assembled unit in both the upper and lower halves. The second and third stage nozzle
segments are assembled to the turbine casing and ellipticity checks are not required.
Assistance from your GE Field Service Representative in obtaining ellipticity readings is
recommended.
1. Set the upper and lower halves of the first stage nozzle on a reasonably level surface and
take ellipticity readings as called for on Inspection Form GT9250.
REASSEMBLY

flanges (one eyebolt for each end of the nozzle). These will be needed after the nozzle
half is partially installed.

assembly, rig to lift the nozzle half inverted (ends pointed down), over the turbine casing.
The lower half of the first stage nozzle weighs approximately 380 pounds. Check to

This document provides information concerning the major tasks and typical responsibilities
associated with a 6001B Major Inspection. It describes the overall work scope, but does not
detail specific methods. Its primary purpose is to provide an overview of a typical inspection
process. Design changes subsequent to the issue date of this document may not be reflected
in this guide.
This document does not purport to cover all aspects of a particular inspection. Unit-specific
details are provided in the document and drawing packages supplied with each requisition, and
all sketches and descriptions are to be considered “Typical.” This document is property of
General Electric and is considered Company Proprietary Information.
HEALTH AND SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
The GI&FS Environmental Health & Safety Manual (EHSM) outlines the requirements that must
be followed on the job site during an installation or maintenance outage.
Safety, health, and protection of the environment must be an integral part of all business
operations, design, construction and start-up, and includes EHS planning prior to and during
work to anticipate and minimize hazards and incidents. Every reasonable effort must be made
to create and maintain a safe and healthy work environment at each customer site.
Where working conditions are not covered by these safety requirements and procedures, or
when a requirement or a procedure is not completely understood, obtain specific instructions or
clarification from manager, supervisor or EHS before proceeding with the work.
INTRODUCTION
This Maintenance Procedure currently exists as a part of a Gas Turbine Service Manual, and is
intended to establish a consistent approach to the performance of flange-to-flange maintenance
inspections for a MS6001B gas turbine. This procedure is intended to consolidate actual field
experience and other maintenance related information normally available only from widely
diverse sources. As maintenance experience is gained on this unit, this procedure will be
supplemented with additional information and descriptions of the work to be performed. This
article currently provides inspection information for Major Inspection workscope. The
procedures described in the text do not supersede or replace specific product department
documentation.

OPERATION 1 - PERFORM ALIGNMENT CHECKS PRIOR TO UNIT DISASSEMBLY
It is suggested that assistance be obtained from your GE Field Service Representative
when performing alignment checks.
1. Remove the load coupling guard and screen.
2. Remove the accessory coupling guard bottom cover. Remove the bolting from the
accessory gear end of the guard and the two top bolts which connect the guard to the
turbine end coupling guard section. Lift this section off.
3. Remove the bolting from the turbine end of the coupling guard and lift off this section.
4. Bag all removed hardware and identify for reassembly.
5. Check turbine to load gear alignment.
Use the hydraulic ratchet to rotate the unit for turbine to load gear alignment
checks. Indicate both face and rim readings on the stationary load gear rotor.
a. Check alignment of turbine to load gear at the load gear end of the load coupling.
This allows an alignment procedure which is identical to the one employed during
installation. The turbine to load gear coupling must be unbolted and jacked apart.
Matchmark load coupling prior to unbolting and jacking apart.
The output coupling is accessible for removal and replacement during
major inspection since the exhaust frame is disassembled, however
special fixturing (tooling) is provided to remove and replace the output
coupling and to disassemble and assemble the number 2 bearing with the
exhaust frame in place.

b. Position a dial indicator for a vertical reading on the O.D. of the load coupling every
45°. Rotate turbine rotor and record the opening coupling runout on GT5025. Refer

The generator field and load gear do not have a thrust bearing;
therefore, there will be a tendency for the rotor to "walk" axially.
Caution

All readings must repeat three consecutive times to be considered
accurate. The indicators should return to "0" (corrected reading of zero for
the face and rim indicators) when returning to the top end of the vertical
mark. If they do not, check tightness of set-up and repeat the readings.

d. Record coupling alignment readings on Inspection Form GT1010. Refer to MLI

a. Using a felt tipped pen, mark two lines (one vertical, the other horizontal) across the

OPERATION 15 - TAKE ROTOR THRUST AND COMPRESSOR CLEARANCES
1. To take rotor thrust clearances, mount a dial indicator on the number 1 bearing housing,
to be able to read axial movement of the turbine rotor.
Do not use any stationary reference point other than the number 1 bearing
housing so as to prevent erroneous readings.
2. Move the rotor axially with a small hydraulic ram and blocking between the inlet casing
and the compressor rotor toward the exhaust end of the turbine until the rotor "bumps"
against the "unloaded" thrust face. Set the dial indicator to zero.
3. Move the rotor axially toward the compressor inlet, using a small ram and blocking
between the load gear coupling and the forward load gear bearing housing. The rotor
should be firmly against the "loaded" thrust face but not loaded so as to deflect the
bearing or casings when the indicator is read.
4. Read the amount of rotor movement as shown on the dial indicator.
5. The range of axial movement of the rotor without distorting the rotor or bearing mounts is
usually between 0.014 and 0.020 inch. Repeat the rotor thrust check at least three (3)
consecutive times in order to assure repeatability.
6. Record thrust movement and compressor clearances on Inspection Form GT7200.
All axial compressor clearances are to be measured with the rotor in contact with
the forward or "normally loaded" face of the thrust bearing.
7. Measure and record stator blade tip clearances for all seventeen compressor stages (S1
to S17).
8. Measure and record compressor rotor blade tip clearances for all seventeen compressor
stages (R1 to R17).
9. Measure and record exit guide vane stator blade clearances (EGV1 and EGV2).

Lube oil contamination with dirt or metal particles will result in scored surfaces of
rotor journals, thrust faces, bearing liners, and thrust bearings. A characteristic
of particle scored bearings is the frequent occurrence of full circumferential score
marks on the rotating members. On journal and thrust bearing liners the score
marks will frequently extend through the circumferential length of the pressure
zone. Although damage to bearing surfaces will result in a theoretical
performance degradation, certain practical limits can be set within which the
function of the bearing is not compromised beyond the degree normally expected
from manufacturing variables. A restricted number of circumferential grooves
can therefore be tolerated in the bearing area provided the total volume of the
groove (which acts as a partial oil short-circuit) is limited. The following are
acceptance limits which can be used as an acceptance guide for used bearing
components.
6. Some scratching or pitting will always occur on babbitted bearing surfaces during normal
operation because of impurities which accumulate in the lubricating oil system. Scratches
or pits that are not over 0.005 inch deep, pits that are not over 0.100 inch in diameter and
pits or scratches do not extend axially more than 1/3 of the bearing length, (axial
scratches and pit formations must be circumferentially at least 45° apart), are acceptable.
Raised metal is not allowed.
The cumulative width of all scratches in circumferential and axial directions
should not exceed 0.100 inch. (Circumferential or axial pit formations exceeding
three in number must be counted as continuous scratches.) Raised metal may
be removed by scraping or lightly polishing the affected area with plastic wool
such as "Scotchbrite." Damage that exceeds the specified limits requires
replacement of the bearing liner.
7. If the bearing liner has experienced excessive temperatures, the babbitt will show
evidence of smear and wiping. If the wiped area is less than five percent of the liner
lower-half area, the bearing may be reused after re pair of the wiped surface. Larger
wiped areas must be repaired by an approved GE Repair Facility. Before replacing the
liner, the cause of the wipe must be determined and corrected.
8. Most journal bearings develop polished areas during low speed cranking or coastdown
conditions. The polished area is usually found at the bottom centerline of the bearing liner
and should extend along the entire length of the bearing. This type of pattern is normal
and should not be cause for any alarm. If, however, the polished area is found only on
one edge of the liner, or if it appears on the liner upper half, a problem is indicated which
must be corrected to prevent eventual bearing wipe.

DESIGN AND ERECTION PHILOSOPHY
Equipment Design Philosophy
The 550 Generator is a hydrogen gas-cooled unit with a separate liquid cooling system for
the armature windings. The casing and shields at each end are of welded gas-tight
construction. The two-pole rotating generator field is supported in elliptical journal
bearings mounted in the end shields. A pair of babbitted rings in each end shield are
supplied with oil at a pressure slightly above internal gas pressure to provide a seal for the
hydrogen gas. Heat is removed from the field by the circulation of hydrogen gas through
the stator and rotary field. The hydrogen gas is cooled by passing through horizontal
coolers located in two domes on top of the stator frame. The main power leads are
brought out of the casing through six porcelain high voltage bushings.
Erection Philosophy
Throughout erection of the generator, a high level of cleanliness must be maintained to
ensure that no dirt or foreign matter is introduced into the generator, and that no tools are
left inside the core.
Due to the physical size and weight of the generator, the component parts are shipped
separately and erected on site. This philosophy takes into consideration the constraints
imposed by the weights and physical size of the component parts of the generator.
The lower frame extension contains factory-assembled high voltage bushings. In order to
stay within shipping limitations, the lower frame extension is shipped separately from the
generator stator. After insertion of the generator field is completed on site, the lower
frame extension is raised into position, bolted to the underside of the generator stator, and
seal welded.
GE Energy Services

COMPANY PROPRIETARY INFORMATION
Field Engineer's Manual – Gas Turbine EM 5487
February 29, 2000
Subject Generator (Model 550) Centerline Assembly Page 6
The generator stator is lifted and placed on the foundation using special heavy lifting
equipment. The rotating field is then lifted and handled using the turbine building
overhead crane. After setting the stator, the rotating field is inserted into the stator and
the end shields are erected. One electrical connection to each winding lead is then made
inside the lower frame extension using bolted flexible connectors. Near completion of
mechanical assembly, the end shield piping is assembled.
At this point the brush rigging is installed. Finally, the stator frame lagging is erected and
fit between the collector house and the steam turbine lagging.
Note: Use only turbine oil to lubricate generator bolting. Do not use metallic thread
lubricating compounds of any kind.

HEALTH AND SAFETY REGULATIONS IN THE U.K.
The Health and Safety Regulations for the UK must be observed during installation of this
equipment. Copies of these regulations will be supplied on site by General Electric’s consultant
(Bucknall Austin). The section covering this article is "Construction - Health, Safety and Welfare
Regulations, 1996."
RECEIVING, HANDLING AND STORING EQUIPMENT
The equipment and materials defined in this instruction can normally be stored in an outdoor
laydown area with suitable cribbing to elevate the equipment above ground and with adequate
weather protection provided (i.e., tarps). Other specific storage or preservation instructions from
the Owner or the GE Technical Advisor shall also apply if applicable. All material received shall
be stored and arranged to accommodate the correct order of installation. Refer to the detailed
erection procedures referenced herein, and to GEZ 5691H, Protection of Steam Turbine and
Generator Components During Shipment and Startup.
Inventory of Equipment
The Installer is to perform a detailed inventory of all material against the shipping packing
lists provided. In the event a discrepancy, a Discrepancy Report is to be issued. All
discrepancies are to be reported immediately to the GE Technical Advisor for verification
and assistance in initiating corrective action and filing claims.
All shipping damage or shortages are to be reported immediately to the GE Technical
Advisor for verification and assistance in initiating corrective action and filing claims.
Preliminary Work
Prior to commencing with any erection activities, the following preliminary work activities
must be completed.
Review of Erection Documentation
1. Review all erection documentation as referenced in this instruction.
Preparation of Work Area
1. Verify that the turbine building overhead crane has been load tested and is
operational.

EQUIPMENT ERECTION SEQUENCE
Throughout the field assembly, refer to MPL Item D5B, Field Assembly and Disassembly -
Notes, and to D5BA, Field Assembly and Disassembly. In the following sections, all Item Nos.
mentioned in parentheses ( ) refer to these two drawings. See Figures 5 and 6.
The recommended sequence of erecting the generator is as follows.
1. Preliminary placement of the Lower Frame Extension.
2. Set the Generator Stator (see EM 5486).
3. Remove the temporary End Covers.
4. Install the Inner and Outer End Shields.
5. Install the Generator Field.
6. Align the Generator Field Coupling (per EM 5490).
7. Install the Cooler Bundles into the Stator Dome Coolers.
8. Install the Stator Dome Coolers.
9. Install the Collector Enclosure.
10. Erect the Lower Frame Extension.

Preliminary Setting of the Lower Frame Extension
The lower frame extension must be positioned in the generator pit prior to setting the
generator stator.
Set the lower frame extension on cribbing in the bottom of the generator pit.
Setting the Generator Stator
Setting the generator stator is detailed in EM 5486, MS9001H D-10 Steam Turbine and
550 Generator Centerline Equipment Rigging.
Removing the Temporary Covers
The generator is shipped with temporary steel covers over the ends of the generator
stator. These shipping covers must be removed prior to insertion of the generator field.
1. Remove the temporary shipping covers.
2. Clean the Stator to End Shield mating surfaces.
Installing the Inner and Outer End Shields
1. Tools for installing the Generator outer and inner end shields and field into the stator
are found in MPL Item B8HO, Assembly Device List.
2. The generator end shields are shipped as complete assemblies with bearings, oil
deflectors, and hydrogen seals installed. It will be necessary to partially
disassemble these parts and to reassemble them on the generator stator after the
field is inserted. Clean and mark all parts and hardware for re-assembly.
3. Protect the stator frame mounting surface using a protective shim.
4. Install the lower end shields at the turbine and collector ends in the lowered position
using the lowering brackets (13).
5. Assemble the supporting bracket (1) of the field supporting sling to the collector end
of the stator frame.

Installing the Generator Field
Note: Prior to inserting the generator field into the stator, the generator RTDs and TCs
should be checked for continuity and function. The generator field should not be
installed until all problems with RTDs and TCs are addressed and resolved.
1. Insert the flexible fiber protective shim (2) into the air gap. Grease the inner surface
of the steel air gap shim (3) lightly with D6A2C1 (paraffin wax), and place it on the
protective shim (2).
2. Ensure that the steel air gap shim (3) is placed with the pulling holes outside the
stator core.
3. Verify that all cables are removed from the air gap shim prior to inserting the
generator field.
4. Insert a wooden brace (6) between the air gap shim and the end shield so that the
shim does not move during insertion of the generator field.
5. With the aluminum covers (28) in place at the middle of the field, and with hitches
(7, 8) around the generator field body so that the vertical centerline through a field
pole will be at the bottom of the field (as shown in section A-7), enter the field into
the core (Position A).
WARNING: Extreme care must be taken when inserting the field into the
stator. It is critical that the rotor coupling and the retaining
rings do not contact the stator core punchings, as damage to
these critical components may occur.
6. Raise the field and insert the Textolite coupling shoe (4). Place the weight of the
field on a wooden block (9). The generator field is now supported by the coupling
shoe and suitable wooden blocks under the collector end journal. Remove the
rigging cables and the protective aluminum cover from the generator field.
7. Rig a suitably sized chainfall and cable between a secure fixed point axially in line
with the generator coupling. This chainfall will be used to slide the generator field
into the stator while it is resting on the coupling shoe or lower body shoe.

8. Using the cable (10), raise the collector end of the generator field (using a copper

9. Using the axial chainfall installed previously, slide the generator field on the coupling

generator field shoe. Refer to MPL D5B, Section D3 or D5. The house crane will
periodically need to be moved toward the generator following the field. (Failure to

10. With the collector end sufficiently raised, insert the field shoe with the dowels

11. Slide the generator field on the shoe until approximately 1 inch (25.4 mm) of space
is attained between the generator coupling and LP Steam Rotor flange.
Note: Extreme care must be used not to nick or damage the coupling face.
12. Assemble the field supporting sling (11) to the supporting bracket (1) at the
generator collector end. Support the collector end of the field in the sling and center
the field using a protective copper shim to protect the journal.
Installing the Generator End Shields
1. Inspect the end shield flange face and rabbet fit for high spots and burrs. Remove
as necessary.
2. Raise the turbine end lower end shield (15) and install per P12A-AL-0223, Outer
End Shield Assembly and Sealing Procedures. Clean the bolting surface and apply
a light coat of turbine oil on the vertical joint and horizontal joints. Ensure that
turbine oil does not get into pumping grooves. Assemble the end shield in position
on the stator frame. (The end shield has been assembled, aligned and doweled at
the factory.) End shield installation is extremely critical. Carefully follow instructions
in P12A-AL-0223. Ensure that the dowels are installed in their original locations as
indicated by the stamping on each dowel. Adjustable bushing bolts may be used to
position the end shields and ease dowel installation. Torque bolts in sequence per
P12A-AL-0223. Torque values for steel generator joint bolts are given in the
following table.

4. Raise the collector end end shield (15) and assemble in position on the stator frame

5. Assemble the jacking device (17) on the collector end lower-half end shield. Fasten
the bottom ring to the outer oil deflector bolt circle using hex head cap screws and
plain washers. Rig and lift the bottom ring into position using two 1 1/4 x 7 inch eye
bolts. Ensure that all cap screws (13) and washers are used to secure the bottom
ring to the end shield. Lubricate the cap screws before installation and torque to
180 ft./lbs. (244 nm). Clean the jack and lubricate with extreme pressure lubricant
or approved anti-seize compound before installing in the lifting yoke. Rig and lift the
lifting yoke into position on the bottom ring using two 3/4 x 10 inch eye bolts. Before
lifting the field with the lifting device, place the copper shim (20) under the generator
shaft to protect its surface finish.
6. Rig up and roll in the lower half of the turbine end ring and bearing. Use two 1 1/2 x
6 inch shoulder eye bolts to lift the bearing half. Lubricate the ball fit and journal
surface with oil (type 600 SSU @100F) before rolling the bearing into the bearing
ring. Ensure that the bearing is correctly oriented according to the rotation arrow
marked on the side of the bearing. Roll the bearing in slowly and carefully,
maintaining control by using the two 1 1/2 x 6 inch shoulder eye bolts screwed into
the outside diameter at the 40 degree position.
7. Install the lower-half collector end bearing (this is an insulated bearing) using the
same procedure as for the turbine end bearing. Ensure that the insulation is not
damaged during assembly.
8. Lower the rotor into the bearings and make bearing tilt/twist checks and adjustment.
At this time, preliminary tilt and twist checks can be made using feeler gauges.
Check between journal and bearing working at four at the horizontal joint. Refer to
GEK 46097D for tilt/twist limits and calculations.
The bearings must be in place to obtain an accurate rotor position for setting the
inner oil deflectors. After the inner oil deflectors are set, the bearings must be
removed to gain access for installation of the hydrogen seals. The bearings are
then reinstalled. Final tilt/twist checks are made using lead wire as described in
GEK 46097D.

This procedure has been written to provide guideline information to help the field engineer install
the Dry Low NOx system on an MS6001 natural gas fuel machine. This procedure was written
for a unit that shipped without the combustion system installed and for a unit that is going to be

system, cooling and sealing air system and air extraction system, cooling water system, piping

Subject "DLNx-1" Control System Page 1
GENERAL
The purpose of the Dry Low NOx (DLNx) control system is to regulate the distribution of the fuel
and the location of flame in the staged multi-nozzle combustors around the gas turbine. A
diagram of a DLNx I combustor is provided in Figure A.
GAS FUEL SYSTEM
A schematic of the DLNx gas fuel delivery systems is shown in Figure B. The fuel system is
made up of the gas fuel speed/ratio valve, the gas control valve, the gas splitter valve, and the
gas transfer valve.
The speed/ratio valve (SRV) is designed to maintain a predetermined pressure, P2, at the
control valve inlet. The gas control valve (GCV) regulates the desired overall gas fuel flow
delivered to the turbine in response to the command signal FSR from the SPEEDTRONIC
panel.
The total gas flow is separated into three stages by the DLNx I system valves, the gas splitter
valve (GSV) and the gas transfer valve (GTV). The DLNx I valves control the percentage of the
total fuel flow delivered to the different stages of the DLNx I multi-nozzle combustor.
The gas splitter valve (GSV) regulates the distribution of the fuel flow to the primary and
secondary zones in the combustor. The gas transfer valve (GTV) divides the fuel supplied to
the secondary zone between two separate flow paths in the secondary fuel nozzle. The
secondary fuel nozzle assembly contains a flow passage that mixes air and fuel ("secondary"
nozzle) and a normal diffusion type passage ("transfer" nozzle).
LIQUID FUEL SYSTEM (IF APPLICABLE)
The liquid fuel system, is composed of the liquid fuel stop valve, main fuel pump, control valve,
fuel filter, flow divider, and the liquid fuel splitter valve. The fuel pump and control valve work in
conjunction with the flow divider and a number of orifices in each secondary fuel line to supply
each combustion chamber with the required fuel flow.
Liquid fuel can be supplied to a set of liquid fuel nozzles in the primary zone and a nozzle in the
secondary zone of the DLNx I combustor. The liquid fuel splitter valve is an on/off type valve
that is used to divert a fixed percentage of the total fuel flow down the secondary zone flow
path. Typically, an orifice in the liquid fuel piping is sized to govern this fixed percentage
through pressure flow division.

FLAME DETECTION
Reliable detection of the flame location in the DLNx I system is critical to the control of the
combustion process and to the protection of the gas turbine hardware. Four flame detectors in
separate combustion chambers are mounted to detect primary zone flame. Four additional

Subject "DLNx-1" Control System Page 3
flame detectors in separate combustion chambers are dedicated to detect secondary flame.
The signals from these flame detectors are processed in control logic and used for various
control and protection functions including the DLNx combustion mode determination.
IGNITION SYSTEM
Two spark plugs located in different combustion chambers are used to ignite the fuel flow in the
primary zone of the combustors. These spark plugs are energized to ignite the fuel during
startup and during certain DLNx I mode changes that require re-ignition of the primary
combustion zone. Flame is propagated to those combustion chambers through crossfire tubes
that connect the primary zones of adjacent combustion chambers around the gas turbine.
Flame is introduced in the secondary zone of the combustion chambers by igniting the
secondary fuel flow with flame from the primary zone.
GAS FUEL OPERATION
The gas turbine firing temperature is defined as the temperature at the inlet to the first stage
turbine nozzle. Due to the extreme temperatures in this region of the gas turbine, it is
impractical to measure the firing temperature directly. The SPEEDTRONIC control software
calculates a turbine firing temperature through known thermodynamic relationships by
measuring the gas turbine exhaust temperature, the compressor discharge pressure and the
ambient temperature.
The fuel flow split between the DLNx I combustion chamber fuel nozzles and the location of the
flame (DLN mode) is regulated as a function of the calculated turbine firing temperature signal
(TTRF1).
There are four basic modes of distributing the fuel to the DLNx I combustor (Figure B1).
Primary
Fuel and combustion are only in the primary zone. Primary combustion is from ignition to
full speed then through approximately 35% load or 1500F* firing temperature.
Lean-lean
Fuel and combustion are in both the primary and secondary zones. Typical load is 35%-
70% and firing temperature in lean-lean mode is from 1500F to 1850F*.

NOTE: Premixed Operation can be extended to lower load ranges with reduced Inlet Guide Vane Operation
Figure B1 Fuel Staged Dry Low NOx I Gas Fuel Operating Modes
Secondary
All fuel and combustion is transferred to the secondary zone of the combustor, through the
transfer manifold. Secondary mode is a transitory mode to extinguish the primary flame
during the transfer from Lean-lean to the Premix mode of operation. Typical firing
temperature for this transition is 1850F*.
Premix
In this mode, fuel is in introduced in both the primary and secondary zones, with
combustion only occurring in the secondary zone. Air and a majority of the fuel are mixed
in the primary zone and combustion occurs only in the secondary zone. "Premixing" the
air and fuel reduces gas turbine exhaust NOx emissions. This mode of operation is
typically from 70%-100% load or above 1900F firing temperature.

temperature. During normal loading of a unit operating on gas fuel, the system will
progress through Primary, Lean-Lean, Secondary and Premix modes. Normal unloading
of the machine from high loads on gas fuel will go from Premix to Lean-lean after the
spark plugs re-ignite the primary combustion zone. Further unloading will cause Primary
mode operation to be initiated which will continue through breaker opening until turbine
shutdown.
During the transfer from Lean-Lean to Premix, the gas transfer valve splits the gas fuel
flow in the combustors’ secondary stage fuel nozzle between the premixing "secondary"
passage and the diffusion "transfer" passage. It is necessary to route some of the
secondary fuel flow through the diffusion section of the secondary nozzle during this
transfer period in order to lower combustion dynamics and stabilize the secondary flame.
Figure C Liquid Fuel Splitter Valve Schedule
Figure C is a typical trace of the DLNx I valve positions during the transfer from Lean-lean
to Premix mode*. The gas transfer valve will normally be in the 0% stroke position,
meaning that 100% of the secondary fuel flow will be to the secondary premixing passage
in the secondary nozzle assembly. During transfer to the Secondary mode of operation,
flame is extinguished in the primary zone by the gas splitter valve diverting all flow to the
secondary zone. In Secondary mode, to accommodate the higher flow of fuel flow
through the secondary, the gas transfer valve will move to an intermediate position in
order to route part of the secondary fuel flow through the diffusion passage.
After flame has been extinguished in the primary combustion zone, the machine transfers
into the Premix mode of operation. The gas splitter valve moves to re-admit fuel into the
primary zone and the gas transfer valve ramps to a position that will cause the secondary

LIQUID FUEL OPERATION (WHEN APPLICABLE)
In the DLNx I system, liquid fuel combustion occurs in either the Primary mode or the Lean-
Lean mode. The DLNx I combustor is ignited during startup and operated in the Primary mode
up to full speed no-load.
When the calculated firing temperature reaches a set value at some part load point, the liquid
fuel shear valve will open and divert a fixed percentage of the total fuel flow down the liquid fuel
passage in the secondary nozzle assembly. Diverting some of the total fuel flow into the
secondary zone is necessary to prevent primary zone flame from damaging the combustion
liner venturi which separates the primary and secondary zones.
Normal unloading of the turbine on liquid fuel from base load progresses at a constant split
between primary and secondary fuel flow until a firing temperature setpoint causes the liquid
fuel shear valve to shutoff the secondary fuel flow. The turbine is then unloaded and shutdown
in the Primary mode.
