PURGE SYSTEM
With all DLN, the purge system is a critical part of the combustion and controls system. Purge
air is used to cool the nozzles as well as keep back pressure from forcing fuel back into the
manifolds where it could ignite and cause substantial damage to manifolds, piping or even the
turbine. During fuel transfers and steady state operation, it is imperative that fuel not be allowed
to enter an unused nozzle or manifold and ignite.
The purge system, which uses compressor discharge air on gas fuel and atomizing air for liquid
fuel, consists of stop valves, limit and pressure switches, all of which provide feedback to the
turbine control system. Because the purge system is connected directly to the fuel gas
manifold, it is important to maintain a system of checks that will not allow the fuel to work
backwards into the purge system and thus the compressor discharge casing, where it could
ignite. These checks, on gas fuel purge, are accomplished through use "double block and
bleed" purge system. Through the use of limit and pressure switches, the turbine control
system ensures the correct position of the purge valves.
IGV TEMPERATURE CONTROL
With all DLN systems, calculated firing temperature is used to determine transfer points
between operating modes. When calculating firing temperature (TFRFI) air flow through the
turbine is one of the critical parameters in determining the maximum firing temperature. For this
reason, the unit must be run with IGV temperature control turned ON, whenever operating in
DLN mode. Running in DLN mode with IGV temperature control turned OFF, will lead to
inaccurate firing temperature calculations and possibly overfiring of the combustion
components.

A system of nomenclature known as "Device Function Numbering" has been adopted by the
Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) and the American National Standards
Institute (ANSI). It provides a means of quickly grasping the main purpose of any device used
as a part of an automatic and manual station control, supervisory, and associated telemetering
equipment. This system, first developed in connection with automatic switchgear, is now
applied to all types of control, protection and power distribution equipment. It is based on the
assignment of a standard number to each of the several fundamental functions performed by
the component elements of a complete equipment.
These device functions may refer to the actual function the device performs or may refer to the
electrical or application to which the device is responsive. Therefore, there may be in some
instances a choice of the function number used for a given device. The best choice is the one
which is recognized to have the narrowest interpretation so that it most specifically identifies the
device in the minds of everyone involved in the design, start-up, operation and maintenance of
the equipment.
The items included in this publication are from IEEE Std. C37.2-1991. Complete copies can be
obtained from The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Inc., 345 East 47th Street,
New York, NY 10017-2394, USA.
The device function numbers with appropriate suffix letter or letters, where necessary, are used
on electrical diagrams, in instruction books and in specifications. Device function numbers,
each with its corresponding function name and the general description of each function, are
listed in this article.
When alternate names and descriptions are included under the function, only the name and
description which applies to each specific case should be used. In general, only one name for
each device, such as relay, contactor, circuit breaker, switch, or device, is included in each
function designation. However, when the function is not restricted to any specific type of device
and where the type of device itself is merely incidental, any one of these alternative names may
be substituted. For example, if a contactor is used in place of a device function 6, starting circuit
breaker, the function name should be specified as Starting Contactor.
